# Stripe Call-Relationship Review

`lib/Customer.php` has long been treated as the legacy entry page for the Customer resource. The page originally served a very narrow purpose: when someone saw the name Customer in existing PHP code and needed to know which file to open first, the index sent them here. The early draft did not produce a method list or preserve a request path; it only copied down the relationships visible in the file header.

The two lines at the entry remain the most stable content on this page:

```php
use ApiOperations\NestedResource;
use ApiOperations\Update;
```

Viewed in the context of the file path, they give us file-level adjacency, not an execution trace with an established order:

```text
lib/Customer.php
├── ApiOperations\NestedResource
└── ApiOperations\Update
```

The old draft once read too much into this small graph, as if Customer's subsequent actions could be inferred directly from the two import names. The review did not uncover such a chain. That assessment needs to be restated: the `use` declaration is first and foremost the source file's import of a name; it helps readers determine which symbols to focus on next, but does not show that any particular request necessarily occurs, nor establish which of the two names is used first at runtime.

This page retains that old interpretation because it explains why the early index grouped Customer, `NestedResource` and `Update` together. For readers who only want to get back to the baseline file, that shorthand remains practical; for those who need to investigate specific behavior, it causes "visible in the same file" to be misread as "a confirmed call." The later review did not fill this gap with guesswork; it only narrowed the reading scope back to the file itself and the two declared neighboring names.

During an actual trace-back, open `lib/Customer.php` first; don't start by searching outward from the resource name. The file path gives the entry point, and the file header gives the two direct dependencies. Then separately verify where `NestedResource` and `Update` are used within the Customer file. Treat them separately: although the two names are listed together in the header, they are independent reading leads and cannot be combined into one action just because they are adjacent in the layout.

If a reference needs to be expanded further, follow that name to the adjacent definition. This lets readers keep "what the file explicitly imports" separate from "what actually appears in the file." The former comes from two `use` declarations; the latter should be determined by the body of Customer inspected in that pass. The early draft did not preserve these occurrence locations, so this page does not pretend to have a method-level map either.

Here, `ApiOperations\NestedResource` means only this: it is one direct dependency name declared in the Customer file header. When you encounter it, return to the Customer file to find the corresponding reference, then decide whether you need to continue reading that name's definition. Do not automatically expand "Nested" in the name into a fixed resource hierarchy; this old record did not retain enough content to support that interpretation.

Handle `ApiOperations\Update` the same way. It appears in the file header and is another lead to trace around Customer; this page does not record it as any specific update request, parameter shape, or caller. When the old index wrote "call relationships," it was actually conflating file-level name relationships with deeper runtime relationships; that is exactly the point that needed a later note.

During the trace-back, you can temporarily stop at three points: the Customer file path, the two `use` declarations, and each one's in-file references. The first two are facts already recorded on this page; the third should be confirmed against the code being viewed each time. These stopping points preserve the old index's value and keep details that were never excerpted from being passed off as long-term conclusions.

This page is not a full resource description of Customer. It records only the starting sequence repeatedly used when dealing with a Legacy Code Reading: start at `lib/Customer.php`, first identify `NestedResource` and `Update`, then expand the two lines outward separately. If the reading goal is only to verify the old entry point, the file header is enough; if the goal is a particular piece of behavior, you still need to return to the Customer body and the relevant definitions.

The neighboring index is retained as DOC-06. It is adjacent to this page but does not replace this page's record of the Customer file's two direct dependencies.

# Stripe Call Flow Notes

This page originally contained only a very rough arrow diagram. Later, someone used it to trace the request path, and only after following it from `lib/Service/CustomerService.php` elsewhere did they realize that the word "entry point" had been given too much weight. The file is still useful to review from the Service side, but it is not a complete call graph.

The earliest margin note is retained below:

> CustomerService is the Stripe call entry point; follow it to see how the request and response flow.

This passage was not removed because it explains why the old links always send people to this file. In hindsight, it conflates three different questions: who initiates a call from the service layer, what object that call uses directly, and where processing continues after the request leaves the service layer. The first two can be checked near the file; the third requires following the call further and cannot be inferred directly from this sentence.

## Order for Reading Through the File

Start at the top of the file and do not immediately search the whole file for "Stripe." The declarations, imports, and object names already present here determine what neighboring relationships can be followed from this page. Then, from each actual call site, inspect a short stretch on both sides: the code before it usually reveals the shape of the arguments the caller passes into the service layer, while the code after it shows whether the call returns the result to the caller or hands it off to another object in the file.

At the time, we did not list all method names in the document. That was meant to keep the old notes from becoming another stale index, but it also left this page with a somewhat inconvenient way to read it: the reader has to open `lib/Service/CustomerService.php` and determine at the specific call site which path they are tracing. When service methods look similar, do not group them into the same request branch based only on the file name.

Temporary annotations can use these categories:

- Where an external caller enters the file, label it "service-side starting point";
- The object directly touched by the current call, label it "neighbor";
- The return, exception, or event-related exit after the call, label it "exit point."

These are code-reading labels only, not type names in the source. Their purpose is to break one path apart: first confirm what step the service file actually performs, then decide whether it is necessary to continue tracing into the request layer, the resource hydration point, or the upstream caller.

## The Old Arrow Diagram

The diagram from the initial draft is still useful, but only for locating the first hop:

```text
Caller
  -> CustomerService
       -> Direct dependency within the file
            -> Request or resource result
```

The last box in the diagram used to read "request or resource result," which is not precise enough in retrospect. A request leaving the service layer and a resource result returning to the caller do not move in the same direction; a call site may expose only one side. During review, this broad wording was retained, and the flow was not extended based on it, because the file itself does not document the entire client path.

Another old conclusion was that as long as the call could be found in CustomerService, the exit for a failed call could also be found in the same code section. That conclusion did not hold up. The surrounding code can help locate handoff points related to failures or events, but whether a visible exception path has actually formed depends on where the specific call leads next. The old notes did not preserve item-by-item results for that part, so we cannot fill in a definite route for every exit.

## How to Use It After Review

Starting from this file is now appropriate in two cases. The first is when the caller already knows it needs CustomerService and only needs to confirm the arguments it receives at the service layer and the object immediately adjacent to it. The second is tracing backward from a resource result, failure symptom, or event exit to find the service-side call site. The two reading paths meet in the same file but diverge afterward; putting them on the same arrow is the most misleading part of the old version of this page.

For the first case, look backward from the call site to verify that the input values were not conflated before the service layer. For the second, look forward from the call site, mark the side where the return or exit is located, and then go back to the actual caller. There is no need to record every neighboring file here just to complete an "end-to-end chain"; this record was never that kind of index in the first place.

DOC-11 preserves the requirements history for Public client symbol map and Int64 scalar and object schema. It is adjacent to this page, but it is not a continuation page of CustomerService: go there when you need to check public symbols, resource objects, or schema; if you are only checking one call relationship in the service file, stay on this page.

Two gaps remain unfilled. First, whether all call sites in the file share the same request-layer branch; second, whether failure and event exits appear as the same kind of return from the upstream caller's perspective. The old page treated both questions as things that would become obvious on their own; after review, we did not retain that assumption. The next time someone opens this page for a specific call, they can add a line beside the corresponding call site instead of rewriting the whole diagram.

This record therefore remains useful for finding the first hop, while it still takes readers back to the old, overly broad wording "call entry point." When citing it, read it together with the correction above.

# Decision on Client Symbols and Int64

We initially grouped public client names and Int64 handling together because both issues could be investigated starting near `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`. The file header contains `use Stripe\Util\Util;`, which only shows that the client layer is adjacent to the utility class; it does not mean that resource classes, numeric rules, and client configuration are implemented in the same place.

At the time, we needed to decide how to document this. We compared three approaches:

1. Center the documentation on the client file, listing configuration, methods, and class names in one table.
2. Organize solely by public name, recording all encountered keys, classes, and methods together.
3. Keep separate records by behavioral boundary: configuration inputs, state reads, resource relationships, scalar conversion, and object conversion.

We chose the third approach.

This was not about the number of names; different failures need separate explanations. The client accepting an array configuration does not mean resources can be loaded; a class name still being present does not mean values inside an object will be converted as expected. The client entry point is the right place to confirm what callers can pass in and read back; the Int64 work should identify where request values and response values each change shape.

The network retry budget was the first example that needed this separation. A budget key in the array only shows that Fang Ke is called to pass in that value; if the client has a separate place to read it, that only shows the value can be retrieved. Without material covering the request path, we do not present those two facts as confirmation of the actual retry count.

The Int64 documentation also starts by distinguishing two cases: a single scalar and an object with members. Someone once suggested recursively processing all numeric-looking strings whenever an object enters the conversion path. That suggestion was not adopted. Object support must identify which members participate in conversion; otherwise, once a field's shape changes, there is no way to tell whether a rule is missing, the payload does not match, or the value should never have been converted in the first place.

The preliminary decision at this point is to keep public names in their respective locations, without treating adjacent appearances as the same compatibility relationship, and to preserve the distinctions between input, output, and object member selection in numeric rules. The details of how to specify object members still need review.
versions.change_summary: Decided to record symbols and numeric rules separately

# Client-Side Symbols and Int64 Decision

Public client symbols and Int64 conversion are still handled on two tracks. Both can appear in the same batch of changes, and both may be discovered near `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`, but they do not answer the same question: one track checks whether callers can continue to pass configuration, read state, or locate public objects; the other checks whether request encoding and response hydration change the shape of values at the designated locations.

The `use Stripe\Util\Util;` in the file header is a clue left by an old troubleshooting entry point. It explains why client issues are often investigated from here, but it does not place resource directories, notification entry points, or schema definitions in this file. Earlier notes turned "can be found from the same place" into "belong to the same batch of compatibility items." That wording is retained below as the starting point for the later correction.

> Old position: As long as the client accepts an array configuration, object names that appear alongside that configuration can be handled together as part of the client compatibility surface.

This rule is no longer used as a basis for deciding. A configuration key describes what calling Fang Ke provides to the client; a resource name describes whether the caller can load, construct, or obtain an object from the payload. The two can change together in one release, but neither proves the other. Future records should first determine whether the issue lies in configuration reading, object export, or value conversion, and only then follow it to the corresponding object.

## Choices Retained During Review

**Aggregate by file.** The entry point is short and suitable for the initial search; the problem is that changes in different namespaces get recorded as a single client change, making it hard afterward to tell whether to change configuration, resources, or encoding logic.

**Build a long table by name.** Classes, constants, array keys, and methods are recorded whenever they appear. This makes searching easier, but conflates "the name still exists" with "the call relationship has been reviewed" as one state.

**Register by boundary.** Configuration entries record the spelling used on input and the read relationship; resource entries record public loading, construction, or hydration relationships; Int64 entries record the conversion scope for inputs, outputs, and object members.

Continue with the third. This split is not intended to add tables; it is to let failures be traced back to the right place: if the expected state cannot be read after configuration is passed in, check the client first; if a class name cannot be found or construction fails, use the resource track; only if an object's field shape is wrong does it fall within the schema scope.

## Scalars and Objects

The second review starts with two shapes: a standalone Int64 scalar and an object with multiple members. The question is no longer phrased as "whether integers are supported," but instead asks separately whether the input needs encoding, whether the output needs hydration, and what determines which members are in scope within the object.

Global automatic conversion was discussed: turn large integers into strings when encountered in a request, and turn strings that look like numbers back into integers in a response. This approach is not adopted. It would erase the path, making it impossible to determine whether a difference comes from a missing schema, a mismatched payload shape, or a field that was never supposed to be converted.

Another candidate was to handle only top-level scalars and have callers preprocess objects. The implementation surface is smaller, but it would leave different callers to define their own rules for object internals. The same payload could produce different shapes through different entry points, and there would be no inspectable object boundary, so it was not adopted.

The retained judgment is: schema nodes must declare the conversion category; objects must identify the members that participate in recursion. Unselected members must not be rewritten merely because they look numeric. This judgment does not establish a field inventory for all objects, nor does it conflate resource exposure with field conversion as a single conclusion.

## One Misjudgment

Accounts, versions, and context often appear in the same request, so an old note once described them as interchangeable client-side auxiliary information. That inference is withdrawn. Calling Fang Ke can read only one of them; an account is not a version, and context is not an alias for either. Even if they appear near a single call in the future, their respective read relationships must be recorded separately.

The network retry budget was also phrased too strongly. The presence of array configuration only shows that the budget can be passed in; the presence of a read entry point only shows that one value can be retrieved. That is not enough to prove that all requests consume that value in some way. The old statement is no longer used to approve client behavior.

## Margin Reminders

Two short notes were left during review:

- A name being findable by the caller does not mean the call result has been preserved.
- An object identifies the recursive locations first; conversion comes afterward.

The first distinguishes public spelling from runtime relationships. The second rejects indiscriminate traversal. They do not replace the later object checks, but they are enough to stop the old entry point from lumping resource, configuration, and field issues into a single conclusion.

The remaining item is the failure behavior when an object's shape does not match. Existing records contain no reusable diagnostic text, so it is not filled in here.

# Client-Side Symbols and Int64 Decision

This record started as an inventory on the client side. It was revisited repeatedly, not because all the issues were in the same file, but because several rounds of changes happened to lead people to start looking near `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`. The `use Stripe\Util\Util;` at the top of the file is still a useful clue: the client layer and utility classes are adjacent here. This is not an indication of the ownership of the resource directory, event namespace, or numeric rules.

Earlier materials overinterpreted this adjacency. Class names, array configurations, context, and integer conversion were written in one table, which looked complete during browsing, but when an actual anomaly occurred, it was impossible to tell which object to inspect first. The original sectioning, review addenda, and withdrawn approaches are retained below; the old paragraphs are not backfilled with today's wording.

## 2023 spring: Inventory Starting from the Client File

There were initially two questions on the table. First, could the client-side names relied on by callers still be found? Second, was there a consistent explanation for how Int64 was handled in individual values and object payloads? At the time, there was not enough material to turn them into one complete rule, so a narrow decision was made first: do not merge the two types of issues based on file location.

The first track was tentatively called public client symbols. It covered configuration passed in by callers, state read during execution, and public objects that could be located directly. The concern here was not how many names appeared around the client, but what role each name served for the caller. Configuration keys could be passed into the client; read methods could provide some kind of state; context objects could be saved or passed along; version information might also be read separately. These cases were adjacent to one another, but did not substitute for one another.

The second track was numeric shape. At the time, all that was known was that a state anomaly had occurred after scalar processing; there were not enough successful and failed samples to determine whether the difference arose in request encoding, response hydration, or traversal of object members. The initial draft left only one constraint: scalars and objects could not share a vague statement that they "support Int64"; if objects were said to be processable, it had to be possible to explain which members participated in the conversion.

Three ways of organizing the material were compared that day.

1. Starting from the client file, list the configurations, methods, and class names that could be found together.
2. Collect only by public name, and register classes, constants, array keys, and functions uniformly.
3. Record configuration, reads, resource relationships, and numeric conversion separately by behavioral boundary.

The third approach was chosen. This choice did not claim that the inventory of all objects was complete; it only avoided turning "the name is still there" into "the original construction, reading, and conversion relationships have all been preserved." The initial draft left two gaps: how the network retry budget would be read after being passed in; and how the object schema would identify recursive members.

## Marginal Wording from the Same-Day Review

The same-day review added no new classes or fields, but circled a sentence that could easily be overextended:

> As long as the client accepts array configuration, the object and resource names appearing near that configuration can be treated as the same set of client compatibility items.
That statement helped with the initial search at the time, but later ceased to be suitable as a basis for a decision. Array-based configuration indicates what callers can supply; resource classes indicate whether callers can load or construct objects, or obtain them from payloads. They may change together in a single release, but there is no reason to treat either as proof of the other.

The review addendum called for separating three types of failure. If the expected state cannot be read after configuration is passed in, go back to the client side first; if a class name cannot be found or construction fails, turn to resource exposure relationships; only if a field value inside an object has the wrong shape should the investigation move to the schema. At the time, the addendum did not list specific methods or freeze field names; it only rejected using a single table of names to cover problems of different kinds.

There was an even shorter note in the margin: "Object support is not number scanning." It addressed an assumption that was easy to slip into at the time: once an object enters the conversion path, recursively process all strings that look like numbers. There were no object samples supporting this approach at the time, nor was it recorded as a decision that had already been made.

## What the old entry point is still used for

The older troubleshooting process still starts at `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`, not because this file owns all compatibility behavior, but because client configuration and several read relationships form a traceable entry point here. When investigating from this entry point, first separate "passing in" from "reading".

The network retry budget is one of the easiest items to overinterpret. A budget key in the array only indicates that the caller Fang Ke can supply a budget; a read site in the client only indicates that a value can be retrieved. Without information about the request path, these two points cannot establish the actual number of retries for each request. The old notes once presented configuration registration as verification of retry behavior, and that wording has been withdrawn.

Account, version, and context should also be considered separately. They may all appear in a single request, but the caller Fang Ke can rely on just one of them. The account value is used for account selection; the version value is used for API version selection; the context object retains request-related state. Describing the continued readability of one item as meaning that the other two also have no compatibility risks is another misjudgment arising from their proximity.

The client file can also help readers confirm where the initial search starts, but should not be treated as a directory of resource classes. Whether a resource can be loaded, constructed, or hydrated from a payload is, in each case, a matter of resource exposure relationships. The client's ability to initiate calls involving these objects does not mean that the client file defines them.

## Fall 2023: Looking at scalars and objects separately again

The second pass started again with two shapes. One was a standalone Int64 scalar; the other was an object with multiple members. The question was no longer framed as "whether integers are supported", but instead separately asked whether request values needed encoding, whether response values needed hydration, and what determined the set of members within an object.

At the time, global automatic conversion was discussed first. The proposal envisioned this: all large integers encountered in requests would be converted into strings, and all strings in responses that looked like numbers would be converted back into integers. Its appeal was that callers would not need to specify field paths; its flaw lay in exactly that. Once path distinctions were erased, it was impossible to tell whether a given discrepancy came from a missing schema, a mismatched payload shape, or a field that should not have been converted in the first place. The proposal was not approved.

The subsequent discussion considered supporting only top-level scalars and leaving objects for callers to preprocess. This narrowed the implementation scope, but left each caller to decide the rules within objects independently. The same payload could take on different shapes through different entry points, and the record could not indicate whether those differences came from caller conventions or client behavior. This approach was therefore not adopted.

The direction retained was narrower: schema nodes declare conversion categories; object nodes identify the members that participate in recursion. Unselected members within an object must not be changed automatically merely because they look numeric. This decision did not establish an inventory of all object fields, nor did it treat resource names as field-selection rules.

The review also recorded a failure case: when the object shape does not match, the result must not be treated as a success simply because the outer object has already entered the path. The available materials provide no error text that can be reused, so no diagnostic is invented here. What value shapes should be preserved for successful and failed calls, respectively, was left as an open question at the time.

## Two reminders from the meeting

The meeting record did not amount to lengthy minutes, leaving only two sentences that were later repeatedly written in the margins:

- A name being discoverable by callers does not mean call results have been preserved.
- First identify the recursion locations within an object, then discuss conversion.

The first sentence separates public spelling from runtime behavior. The existence of configuration keys, accessor methods, class names, and constants can support a name-level assessment; the existence of names cannot establish whether accounts, versions, contexts, or resource objects produce the expected results when called. The second sentence rejects global automatic conversion: if it is unclear which locations in an object are subject to the rules, so-called object support is merely a traversal strategy.

A specific misjudgment arose in the same round of discussion: versions and accounts often accompany requests, so someone assumed that as long as the context object remained readable, it could also indirectly stand in for version access. This assessment was later retracted. Accounts, versions, and contexts may appear together, but a call to Fang Ke may read only one of them; compatibility for one cannot substitute for the other two.

## The old approach left in place

The following passage comes from an old meeting draft. Old links still take readers to similar lists, so the original text is retained; it is not the current approach.

> Place client configuration, resource classes, and the Int64 schema in the same pre-release table, requiring only that each name appear once.

The problem with this approach was not just that the table was too long. A name appearing once cannot indicate whether it is a configuration key, an accessor entry point, a class, a constant, or a schema node; nor can it indicate whether a value is encoded on the request side or hydrated on the response side. When this table was used, resource-loading errors and numeric-encoding errors were often routed to the same entry point, after which the scope could only be narrowed down by guesswork.

The old meeting draft also contained an even earlier idea: automatically derive Int64 rules from the public resource symbol graph. This proposal was not approved. The public loading surface of resources and the encoding rules for fields operate at different levels of granularity. A public resource does not necessarily have Int64 fields; a field that requires conversion may also appear in multiple object shapes. Deriving the schema from the resource catalog would cause resource moves to unexpectedly change encoding decisions.

The reverse does not hold either. A schema describes how values are handled, not whether a class can be publicly loaded, whether a constant is exported, or whether a service entry point exists. Resources and schemas can be examined side by side in the same regression run, but the results for one cannot substitute for those for the other. The old draft once called this side-by-side review a unified compatibility surface, a term that has now been abandoned.

## An object discussion that got out of hand

The object rule was once simplified to "deep-process an object after it enters the conversion path." This description did not explain how members are selected, nor did it handle union shapes. Someone in the discussion tried to make the decision based on whether the object contained numeric strings; this condition is too broad: it can neither preserve field boundaries nor indicate which branch should take effect.

A later addendum did not rewrite this passage into a complete solution; it only identified two gaps: object members need an explicit scope; a union cannot borrow field definitions from another branch. The former addresses indiscriminate recursion, while the latter addresses erroneous merging when objects look similar. Both stem from the same lesson: a value's appearance is insufficient to determine its conversion rule.

At this stage, resource hydration and numeric conversion still had not been put back on the same path. An object may be both the payload of a public resource and contain values that need conversion; this does not mean resource selection can decide the field rules. Resource questions should first confirm the class and hydration relationship, and field questions should then confirm the schema and object shape.

## Correction Record

A subsequent review confirmed that the original direction of "separating by boundary" was not wrong, but the wording was too general. If the client section is written only as a set of symbols, readers will still collapse configuration, reading, and type into a single concept; if the Int64 section mentions only scalars and objects, it will also omit the differences among requests, responses, and unions.

Therefore, the client record was changed to retain four positions: the spelling of the configuration supplied by the caller, the state-reading entry point, the context type, and version metadata. This division does not package them under a new umbrella term; instead, it acknowledges that a call to Fang Ke can depend on only one of them.

The Int64 record was likewise revised to retain four questions: how requests are encoded, how responses are hydrated, which object members participate in the rule, and how a union selects a branch. This is not a requirement that every check exhaustively enumerate all objects; rather, it prevents an anomaly from leaving the only fallback as the vague guess that it "may have something to do with integers."

The state diagram below reflects only the reading order established by this record: first separate client symbol verification from object-field rules, then proceed from object-member selection to the current position.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Client symbol verification
    Client symbol verification --> Separate configuration and reading
    Separate configuration and reading --> Recheck Int64 shapes
    Recheck Int64 shapes --> Object member selection
    Object member selection --> Current position
```

## Current Position

On the client side, compatibility is no longer described as "names being near each other in the same file." Configuration items retain the spelling supplied on input; read items retain the access entry point; contexts retain their type; version metadata retains the public constant. The fact that an array configuration, a read method, and a type name are adjacent in the same call still does not provide grounds for substituting one for another.
The client-runtime compatibility manifest keeps the exact public spellings max_network_retries, getStripeAccount, getStripeVersion, getStripeContext, Stripe\StripeContext, and Stripe\Util\ApiVersion::CURRENT; structured agent metadata uses the ai_agent key.

This decision fixes the spellings and locations that calls to Fang Ke depend on, rather than generalizing them into a single broad accessor. `max_network_retries` is the network retry budget key in the array configuration; how the request layer consumes that value should still be verified along the request path. `getStripeAccount`, `getStripeVersion`, and `getStripeContext` are respectively the entry points for reading the account, version, and context; one of them cannot be used in place of the other two merely because it remains callable.

`Stripe\StripeContext` is the context type that callers can save, pass, and read. Older materials treated it as a temporary container for the account and version, and therefore tried to treat the readability of the two values as a substitute for the object itself; that understanding has been corrected. `Stripe\Util\ApiVersion::CURRENT` retains the public location of the current API release version, requiring the current value to be defined and non-empty; this record does not fix a particular release string.

`ai_agent` in structured client metadata is the field name. When Claude Code is detected, it carries the agent type, with the value `claude_code`. Environment detection may be conditional, but once the data enters structured JSON, the field spelling does not change with the condition.

The current wording of the numeric rules has likewise been narrowed to a checkable form. A node uses `kind` to specify the conversion category; `int64_string` indicates that request values are encoded as decimal strings, and response strings are rehydrated into integers. Object mode uses `fields` to list members that require recursive processing. This key is not an alternative way to scan all object members; unlisted members do not automatically undergo conversion merely because they look like numbers.

A union shape must not be merged as an ordinary object. `discriminatedUnion` represents a discriminated union, and `variants` stores the mapping from discriminator values to the corresponding variant schemas. When a discriminator value does not match, do not borrow field definitions from another branch to construct a seemingly usable object. This restriction comes from the boundary established after the global automatic-conversion scheme was abandoned, not from an attempt to turn schema names into resource directories.

## Adjacent Issue Not Yet Split Off

There is still an adjacent case without enough failure samples: when an object has an Int64 field and is also hydrated through a migrated resource class, how should resource selection and field conversion be presented at the same time without conflating the two types of issues into a single diagnostic? Existing records are insufficient to determine a unified output format, so this question is retained as is.

The event-parsing boundary is also often casually lumped into numeric processing because both touch JSON. They are not the same thing: the event entry point handles the notification type and payload boundary, while the Int64 schema handles the shape of values that have already entered the rule scope. Older records collectively called them decoding rules, making the troubleshooting scope too broad; that terminology is no longer used.

## Appendix of Older Examples

### Resource Names Beside Array Configuration

Early lists placed the resource class name immediately after the network retry budget because callers all started from the client object. This was convenient in terms of layout, but it implied that the two shared an implementation ownership boundary. This example is retained so that people arriving through old links can separate the key, read entry point, and class name again, rather than continuing to add names to the original table.

### Treating Object Processing as Numeric Traversal

Another old example assumed that any object entering an Int64 path could be recursively searched for strings that looked like numbers. It did not distinguish whether a field had been selected by the schema, nor did it represent union branches. That approach was later overturned: object members are constrained by `fields`, and the union selects the corresponding schema from `variants` based on the discriminator value. This appendix preserves the old misinterpretation for the record; automatic traversal should not be restored.

### Reducing Version Metadata to Diagnostic Text

An older version treated version information as a supplement to the release notes and did not include it in public-symbol checks. After it was confirmed that callers read the version metadata directly, the corresponding constant was retained as a separate public surface. This record does not state a specific version number or derive a resource version from the version constant; it only retains the read location that should remain stable on the client side.

# Resource Catalog and Parsing Guardrails Proposal

This round of review covers both resource catalog generation and the V2 webhook parser guard because both affect the entry points callers see, but they should not be treated as a single change.

Keep two candidate approaches under consideration: on the catalog side, organize only public resources and service entry points; on the parsing side, maintain independent guardrails that reject payloads failing the existing checks before they reach the typed notification stage. The cost is that releases need to check the two sets of results separately; checking whether the catalog was generated is not enough.

The initial draft does not yet have enough information to decide which client layer should centrally manage the catalog. `lib/BaseStripeClient.php` is currently the starting point for tracing client-side relationships; the file header shows `use Stripe\Util\Util;`. This is not enough to attribute the resource catalog or the parsing branch directly to that file.

First, capture the visible results of one successful call and one failed call. If those results can only be explained through different entry points, submit the catalog cleanup and parser guard separately. If the guard must depend on object information from catalog generation, withdraw the assumption that they can be split and re-evaluate the costs of a shared entry point.

When the catalog fails, it should be clear whether a resource, service navigation, or response object mapping is missing; a parser guard failure should retain the context that it occurred before notification parsing.

The recheck starts at `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`. This is a suitable starting point for investigating the client side, and it directly uses `Stripe\Util\Util`. The earlier inference that this entry point established catalog ownership was too broad: it can only help confirm relationships around the client, not supply resource definitions for the catalog or payload rules for the parser guard.

We are continuing to trial the two areas separately.

- Keep three checks for the resource catalog: whether public resources can be constructed, whether response object names are hydrated as expected, and whether the client can reach the corresponding services.
- Keep independent checks for the V2 webhook parser guard: exercise the existing parsing entry points with inputs that pass and inputs that fail, and record the affected units and adjacent unchanged units.
- Do not equate "the catalog exists" with "notifications have been parsed safely" in the release notes. The two share a release cadence, but not a success signal.

An earlier idea was to let the catalog generation output directly determine what the parser allows. We are not pursuing that approach at this stage. It would mistakenly treat differences in generated output as payload decisions, and on failure it would be hard to tell whether the catalog was missing an entry or the guard had rejected the payload. Retain the idea and reopen it when we can demonstrate that both sides actually use the same object information.

What is still missing is not more object names, but a minimal record of two calls: one successful catalog-side path, one failing path, and the parser guard's differing behavior on adjacent inputs. # Resource Catalog and Parser Guardrails Proposal

This round reframes the catalog issue from "whether generation is complete" to "which objects callers see through which entry points." Previous notes tended to describe the client, resource classes, and notification parsing as one chain, making it read like a single gap; in actual investigation, they produce different failure signals. The catalog side needs to record the resource name, response object name, and service navigation. The parsing side needs to record whether the guard intercepts the input before the notification object is created.

Near the client, continue tracing back from `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`. Its visible dependency is `Stripe\Util\Util`, so it is suitable for confirming the adjacency relationship on the client-construction side. The previous version treated this path as a candidate location for the catalog implementation; after review, that assessment was revised: this is a navigation starting point, and it should not be expected to own catalog declarations or webhook checks. This correction does not change the trial scope; it only prevents later changes from pushing unrelated responsibilities into the client layer.

## What Each Side Records

A catalog sample needs to answer three questions: whether public resources can be loaded and constructed; whether a response carrying an object identifier hydrates into the corresponding resource; and whether the service can be reached through client navigation. Failure samples should retain the same diagnostic granularity. If all that is recorded is "call failed," later work cannot determine whether to add a resource list, an object mapping, or a service entry point.

For parser-guard samples, the catalog result is not a prerequisite. Run passing and failing inputs through the existing test entry, record the affected parsing units, and retain adjacent unchanged units as well. The guard is meant to prevent payloads that fail the existing checks from continuing into the typed-notification path; it is not an auxiliary check for catalog generation.

This split adds two recording points but reduces misattribution. A missing catalog entry may stop client navigation before the service; a guard rejection may happen before the notification object is created. Collapsing the two phenomena into one "V2 failure" would make the repair direction depend on whichever output happens to be seen first.

## Coupling Approach Not Adopted

At one point, we considered having the generated catalog provide the parser with an allowed scope: one set of object information would determine both service navigation and notification acceptance conditions. The benefit would be one less maintenance surface; the risk is that a catalog-generation error would change parsing behavior, while failure samples would not show whether rejection came from a missing object or an invalid payload.

We are not making this coupling the default. Only when the same object information is genuinely consumed by both sides, and each side's failure signal can be retained, will we compare it again. Otherwise, catalog updates remain catalog updates, and guard changes remain parsing changes. This decision also means that a catalog addition cannot be treated as a basis for the parser guard to pass.

Another approach we did not adopt was to centralize all assertions on the client side. It might appear to let callers check through a single entry point, but it would obscure the difference between resource hydration and service navigation. The client should continue to provide navigation; construction and mapping of concrete objects should still be expressed at their respective locations.

## Catalog Scope Confirmed This Round

The generated-resource catalog resolves Stripe\AccountLink, Stripe\BalanceSettings, and Stripe\Service\BalanceSettingsService, maps financial_connections.authorization to Stripe\FinancialConnections\Authorization, and exposes Stripe\Service\V2\Commerce\ProductCatalog\ImportService through the client navigator.

This sentence limits the catalog's visible results; it does not extend them into webhook payload rules. `Stripe\AccountLink` and `Stripe\BalanceSettings` belong to the resource surface visible to callers (Fang Ke); `Stripe\Service\BalanceSettingsService` and `Stripe\Service\V2\Commerce\ProductCatalog\ImportService`, respectively, indicate that the service entry must still be reachable through navigation. The mapping for `financial_connections.authorization` needs to be observed along the response-object path; service reachability cannot substitute for it.

During the catalog trial, a successful sample should cover at least one complete call chain for one of the three result types above. A failure sample need not use a deliberately complex input, but it should preserve which layer the failure lands in: resource loading, object mapping, or service navigation. When another omission appears, the person making the change can start at the failing layer instead of changing the parser guard first.

## Parser Guard Boundary

The V2 webhook parser guard continues to run independently. The record should include whether the input passes the existing checks, whether parsing continues to create a typed notification, and whether adjacent inputs remain unaffected. Catalog object names can help locate the resource the caller expects, but should not become the parser's payload allowlist.

If a guard test shows that an input that should pass was rejected early, check the conditions near the parser entry first; do not expand the resource catalog first. Conversely, if the client cannot obtain a service or resource, check the catalog and navigation first; do not label it a notification-parsing issue. Both branches need samples before release, but they do not need to use the same input set.

## Items to Retain

- It has not been confirmed whether the generated catalog artifact has a single reusable maintenance point; this does not affect recording resources, mappings, and navigation separately in this round.
- Add a minimal pair of samples: one successful call and one failed call, with the failure layer marked.
- The parser guard's adjacent unchanged units should be retained with the affected units, to avoid expanding the change scope based only on a passing result.

Later, if the catalog and parsing truly need to share object information, reopen the coupling proposal based on failure samples; until then, keep the two change surfaces separate.

# V2 Namespace and Null Troubleshooting Tree

The first symptom was that event-related calls couldn't find the expected object. Don't change the autoload configuration yet; first capture the full name shown in the failure. The old records use `lib/Event.php` as a lookup reference for regular event resources: the file starts with `namespace Stripe;`, has `class Event extends ApiResource` in the middle, and the object is named `event`.

The notes at the time followed two lines of investigation:

- If the caller gets `Stripe\Event`, first check whether the old event constants are still present. `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_AUTHORIZED` and `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_DEAUTHORIZED` can help identify historical event strings.
- If the error text contains a V2 name, don't guess the directory from the location of the old `Event`. First keep the full class name, and wait until you can see the listing before deciding.
- If the input contains an explicit null, first record whether the key exists. A missing key and a key that exists but has a null value are not the same sample.

The initial working assumption was: if the old Event can load, the event issue is most likely still at the regular resource entry point. This assumption is only useful for checking old event strings. It has not been shown to explain V2 names, nor has it been shown that the change in null behavior occurs during resource hydration.

The old page also has a shortcut: check `OBJECT_NAME` first, then trace outward from the account application event constants. This is retained because existing records describe the symptoms using this entry point; when you encounter a full V2 class name, don't use it as a basis for adding an alias.

# V2 Namespace and Null Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally put "name not found" and "explicit null appears not to have been retained" in the same error bucket. After review, both may still occur in the same call, but the evidence to retain is different: the name investigation needs the full class name and where it appeared; the null investigation needs the input structure and the subsequent structure. Without these two sets of evidence, don't write them up as a single root cause.

`lib/Event.php` can still be opened, but only to cross-check legacy regular events. It directly shows `namespace Stripe;`, `class Event extends ApiResource`, and `OBJECT_NAME = 'event'`. Constants for account application authorization and revocation events, as well as external account events, are also here. It can tell you whether legacy event strings are still bound to the regular Event, but not what should be in the V2 directory.

## Start with the Failure Evidence You Have

If the text contains class names, resource names, or export discrepancies:

1. Save the full name, not just a short name such as `Event`.
2. Distinguish whether the name came from the caller, an export list, or a temporary mapping. Identical names do not mean identical sources.
3. When the name is still `Stripe\Event`, you can check the object names and constants in the old file; if the constant exists, stop at the regular event entry point.
4. When the name contains `Stripe\V2\`, check the actual list. If you can't get the list, retain the failing name and stop; don't substitute a similar class name.
5. If a compatibility mapping handles the name, record the mapping itself. A mapping is not evidence of a public export.

If the sample contains an explicit null:

1. First confirm whether the original input actually contains this key.
2. Then check whether the key is still present during request preparation.
3. If the key is still present but its value has changed, retain the before and after structures; if the key is already gone, record whether it disappeared before or during preparation.
4. If the original input does not contain the key, stop classifying it as a passthrough sample.

These branches do not have to be followed to the end every time. For a null record without the original input, all you can write is "Unable to determine whether the key was originally present"; a name record without the full class name can likewise go no further than the original failure text.

## An Old Assessment That No Longer Applies

The early procedure was to first confirm that `Stripe\Event` existed, then go back to the old file for any event class name. This helped when a caller had written `account.application.authorized` incorrectly, but gave a false sense of safety when sorting out V2 names.

**This later stopped applying:** Being able to load the old class only shows that the old class is still there. It does not show that the V2 name exists, nor that the export table contains no old names. One review worked backward from the object name `event` to infer the V2-side name, but ultimately only confirmed that the regular resource was still visible. Expanding the search for old constants did not yield any new directory information either.

Another incident involved an attempt to use a temporary mapping to point the old entry point at the suspected V2 name. The localized failure temporarily disappeared, but subsequent records could not distinguish an actual export from a temporary redirect. That approach was later dropped; in the same situation, you should go back to the list and the failing name rather than adding another mapping.

## Additional Notes on Parameters

Earlier records treated "there is no content in the request" as supporting evidence for null. That wording is too imprecise. A key may be absent from a request because the caller did not provide it, or because something changed during parameter preparation; the old Event file cannot distinguish these two cases.

Only the following narrow branches are retained at this point:

- Original input has no key: not an explicit-null passthrough sample.
- Original input has the key, but it is already absent during preparation: keep the issue scoped to the area around parameter preparation.
- Original input has the key, and the key is still present but its value has changed: retain both structures and continue by checking the request representation.
- Original input has the key, and its value is still null: continue recording the name list and the parameter investigation separately.

Don't replace two records with a single conclusion just because the same call reports both a class-name problem and a null problem.

## Quick On-Call Diagram

```text
Incident evidence
├─ Full class name or list discrepancy
│  ├─ Stripe\Event
│  │  └─ Check old Event constants, only to verify regular events
│  ├─ Stripe\V2\...
│  │  └─ Check actual export names; stop if the list is unavailable
│  └─ Temporary mapping
│     └─ Record the mapping's source; don't treat it as an export
└─ Parameters contain explicit null
   ├─ Original input lacks the key
   │  └─ Stop; this cannot be treated as a passthrough sample
   ├─ Key disappears during preparation
   │  └─ Record the location in parameter preparation
   └─ Key remains but its value changes
      └─ Retain the before and after structures
```

The two sides of the diagram are not interchangeable. The old Event constants can help identify regular events, but cannot fill in the V2 list; a resource sample that loads successfully also cannot show that a particular null-valued key remained unchanged during request preparation.

# V2 Namespace and Null Troubleshooting Tree

This page was originally written for incidents where "the event object suddenly could not be found". Later, explicit null values also appeared in the same set of records, so parameter-related notes kept being added to the margins of the old page. The two lines of investigation have never been shown to involve the same point in the implementation: the former looks at full names and exports, while the latter looks at keys and values in the input. The historical paragraphs have not been removed because some on-call records still contain only an old entry point, an event string, or a vague "event disappeared".

For a new incident, first capture the minimum evidence. For a naming issue, capture at least the fully qualified class name or the original string from the list; for a null issue, capture at least whether the key was present in the original input. Simply writing "V2 event error" is not enough to enter the naming branch; simply writing "null was swallowed" also makes it impossible to tell whether it changed at the caller, during parameter preparation, or around the request representation.

```text
Exception text or parameter sample
├─ Fully qualified class name, resource name, or export differences available
│  ├─ Name is still Stripe\Event
│  │  ├─ Check OBJECT_NAME and the legacy event constants
│  │  └─ Once the constants are confirmed to exist, stop at the regular event entry point
│  ├─ Name includes Stripe\V2\...
│  │  ├─ Save the full string
│  │  ├─ Compare against the actual export list
│  │  └─ If the list is unavailable, retain the name and stop
│  └─ Name is handled by a temporary mapping
│     └─ Record the mapping, do not treat it as a public export
└─ Explicit null appears in the input
   ├─ Original input does not have this key
   │  └─ Stop: not a passthrough sample
   ├─ Key disappears during preparation
   │  └─ Record this at the parameter preparation stage
   ├─ Key is still present, value has changed
   │  └─ Save the structures before and after the change
   └─ Both key and value are still present
      └─ Check the request representation next, do not attribute this to resource loading
```

The diagram marks stopping points for incident investigation, not a requirement to go all the way through every time. For a naming exception without a fully qualified class name, just retain the original failure text; if the original input is not visible for a null sample, you can only state that you cannot determine whether the key was originally present. Do not use legacy Event constants to fill gaps in the name, and do not use a single successful request to fill gaps in the parameter information.

---

## The starting point in 2023: check the legacy Event first

The initial records used `lib/Event.php` as the entry point for event issues. The file contains `namespace Stripe;` and declares `class Event extends ApiResource`. The value of `OBJECT_NAME` is `event`, and the constants for account application authorization and revocation are near that same section. At the time, the problems to address were legacy callers writing regular event strings incorrectly or confusing object names with event types.

The working rule at the time was: if the old Event could load, do not suspect a name migration yet. This rule was useful in practice for ordinary events. When the error text explicitly included `account.application.authorized`, opening the old file to confirm whether it was still bound by `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_AUTHORIZED` was often enough to find that the caller had written the historical string incorrectly.

But this rule was soon applied too broadly. Some people, upon seeing any event class name, would first trace from the object name of old `Event`, and treat a V2 name they could not find as an automatic-loading problem. The old file did indeed contain ordinary event resources, but that did not provide a basis for inferring a V2 directory. We retain the original judgment here to understand why some old records only say "Start with Event."

The initial page also recorded explicit null as an accompanying symptom of the event resource. At the time, there was no structure saved from before and after request preparation, and there was no fragment that could connect parameter changes with name migration. That old statement only shows that the two phenomena were placed on one page by the same on-call shift; it cannot show that they shared a cause.

## On-call marginal notes beside the old file

The on-call notes contain a very terse notation: when the error is `account.application.authorized`, check the corresponding constant in the old file; if the constant is still there, check again whether the caller wrote an ordinary event name as a resource class name. This action can only verify the historical string; it does not generate a new class name or answer which resource the caller should ultimately load.

Another marginal note reads "V2 next to Event." This was not a code conclusion but a directional hint left at the time to shorten the search path. Later, someone used it to look for a directory near the old file and labeled resources that were not found as load failures. Review did not support that attribution.

The marginal note about null was equally crude: "When the input is null, first check whether the request has content." It conflated "the key does not exist" with "the key exists and its value is null." In retrospect, these two inputs need to be distinguished from the outset; the former cannot be a counterexample to pass-through behavior, while only the latter warrants further examination of parameter preparation and request representation.

## A failed attempt to infer the directory from the object name

A later review started with the object name `event` of old `Event`, attempting to derive the name on the V2 side. The result only confirmed that ordinary resources were still ordinary event objects and could not explain the complete V2 names appearing in the manifest. Extending the search along constants such as account application, external account creation, and deletion likewise yielded no directory information.

This attempt left three still-useful stopping points:

- Finding a constant in the old file can only settle the question of whether the old constant has disappeared.
- Not finding a V2 class name in the old file cannot directly be stated as "the V2 class does not exist."
- When the manifest has not been obtained, a similar short class name cannot be substituted for the full name.

There was also a temporary mapping at the time that connected the old event entry point to the suspected V2 name. As a result, one local call no longer failed immediately, but the difference between the exported manifest and the actual loading path was concealed. When the mapping was later removed, the original problem resurfaced. A temporary mapping can be retained as field state; it is not evidence that the name has migrated.

## 2024 annual addendum: Separate null from resource anomalies

After the addendum, samples with explicit null are listed separately at the parameter boundary. For a sample that can be investigated further, at minimum record whether the corresponding key existed in the original input, whether the key was still present during request preparation, and whether the value was still null. When the first two are both absent, do not say that the "key was dropped," nor that it was rewritten during resource construction.

The old "if the request has no content, inspect Event" step is deprecated here. An empty request may mean that the caller did not provide the field, or that the preparation process changed the structure; it cannot, in turn, indicate that the ordinary event resource or the V2 name is problematic.

The branches added at the time were as follows:

1. The original input had no corresponding key: stop. This is not an explicit-null pass-through sample.
2. The original input had the key, but it was already absent during preparation: keep the issue near parameter preparation; do not rewrite it as a resource-loading failure.
3. The original input had the key, and the key was still present during preparation, but the value changed: preserve both structures and continue examining the request representation.
4. The original input had the key, and the value was still null: retain the name list and parameter record separately unless new connecting evidence appears.

This is not a complete explanation of all parameter shapes. It only prevents "missing field," "value transformation," and "class name not found" from being written into the same judgment. For old samples without the original input, retain their original wording; do not fabricate keys and values for them based on the later branches.

## An operation that was crossed out but is still often cited

Below is the operation from the old page, retained for people who need to understand the historical records; it is not a current step:

> First confirm that `Stripe\Event` exists; if it does, map any event class name back to the old file; null in the request can be examined together during object hydration.

At the time, this reduced the number of files that had to be opened, but it collapsed three boundaries into one: whether the old name was still usable, whether the V2 name had been exported, and whether the parameters retained explicit null. It was later crossed out not because the old Event disappeared, but because the three issues require three different types of evidence.

If theon-site team provides an ordinary event string, the old file is still useful. If theon-site team provides a complete V2 class name, the old file can only serve as a counterexample for "do not misuse the old entry point." If theon-site team contains only null, by default do not open the Event file; first inspect the original parameter structure, then determine during which segment the key and value changed.

## Constraints left by the review meeting

The review feedback explicitly requires that `lib/Event.php` not be listed as the source for the V2 catalog. The facts supported by this file are very limited: the old namespace is `Stripe`; the regular `Event` class inherits from `ApiResource`; the object name is `event`; and several historical event strings are retained. It does not provide all the resources in the V2 manifest, nor does it explain the final behavior of null on every request path.

The meeting also corrected a common claim: "If the old class can be loaded, the migration is compatible." Here, "compatible" does not specify whether it refers to names, construction, resource hydration, or parameter handling, so it cannot be used directly as a troubleshooting conclusion. When you encounter this kind of description, first break it back down into answerable questions: which fully qualified name is being loaded, or which parameter key changes in the subsequent structure.

This correction points to the manifest checks that follow, and does not require removing the old entry point. If a legacy call reports a plain event string or `Stripe\Event`, still perform the minimal checks using the old constants; there is no need to recast a legacy error as a V2 symptom just because the current namespace exists.

## Actions for the name track during troubleshooting

When the logs, call stack, or caller explicitly provide a fully qualified V2 name, proceed in the following order:

- Preserve the name verbatim. `Event`, `EventDestination`, and the notification object have similar short names, so comparing them after removing the namespaces can easily lead to misidentification.
- Record where the name appears: caller source code, the manifest, failure text, or a temporary mapping. Do not put all four types of source in the same column.
- If the target name is in the manifest but loading still fails, record where the failure occurs; do not go back to the old Event constants to explain the loading failure.
- If the manifest still contains the old name when the new name is expected, record where the old name appears; do not complete the manifest using another similar class.
- If all you have in the current case is "event resource missing" without a fully qualified name, go back to the trigger point to obtain the name. If you cannot obtain it, stop, and do not associate it with a particular V2 resource.

"The name appears in the manifest" and "the caller has successfully obtained the object" must also be kept separate. The former answers whether the exported text exists; the latter concerns the caller's actual behavior through the public resource entry point. The old page combined the two into a single confirmation, causing the mere appearance of a name to be treated as successful execution. This wording is no longer used.

## Actions for the null track during troubleshooting

The null track does not require opening the old Event file unless there is also a name error in the same case. When preparing samples, retain only the original keys, and do not add extra fields just to make comparisons easier. The focus is on identifying the stage after which the same key is no longer null or no longer exists.

If the key is already absent when the caller constructs the parameters, record the structure supplied by the caller, and do not pass the sample along for an encoding-based explanation. If the key disappears after request preparation, first preserve the parameter structure seen during the preparation stage; "the request does not contain the key" is only an observation and does not explain why it disappeared.

If the key is still null but the request layer behaves differently, preserve the structures on both sides and stop at the request representation. Do not describe it as a resource hydration error, as resource hydration deals with a problem in the other direction.

When class-not-found and null appear together, follow the branch with complete evidence first. Only when the same call site records both the full class name and the parameter structures before and after should they be listed together in the same incident record; even then, record the assessments and unknowns separately.

## What the old resources can answer

The following items come from the old Event file and can still be used to identify historical entry points:

- The namespace is `Stripe`, not a V2 subnamespace.
- `Event` extends `ApiResource`.
- The value of `OBJECT_NAME` is `event`.
- `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_AUTHORIZED` binds `account.application.authorized`.
- `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_DEAUTHORIZED` is still the cancellation type constant for regular events.
- There are also constants related to external account creation and deletion nearby in the file.

These items are used to narrow down the scope of old calls, not as a V2 export table or as rules for handling explicit null. If a historical record treats any constant as proof that migration is complete, label that as an old assessment alongside the original record rather than copying it into a new incident record.

## Old entry-point checks that can still be used

When the observed name clearly points to the old regular Event, the old file is sufficient for a quick check: confirm that the object name and historical constants are still present, then refer the issue back to the point where the caller uses the name. There is no need to expand the V2 directory here.

When the observed name clearly points to V2, the old file serves only as a reference to avoid misclassification. What needs to be recorded is the full name in the manifest, along with whether it is a current name, an old name, a temporary mapping or a missing item. If the name is incomplete, it is better to draw no conclusion.

When the incident involves only null, do not use the old file as the default entry point. First preserve the original parameter structure, then determine where to look next based on whether the key exists and whether the value remains null. This avoids once again recording a parameter anomaly as an event migration failure.

## Current manifest criteria

Following a subsequent review, manifest checks no longer depend on the location of the old `Event`, and using old classes to fill gaps in the new directory is not accepted. The V2 namespace manifest exports Stripe\V2\Core\Event, Stripe\V2\Core\EventDestination, Stripe\V2\Core\EventNotification, and Stripe\V2\DeletedObject, while the pre-migration Stripe\V2\Event class is no longer exported.

When a name fork contains `Stripe\V2\Core\Event`, record it using the complete resource name in the checklist, not an abbreviation to the generic Event. When `Stripe\V2\Core\EventDestination` appears, retain the complete path, without inferring its existence from old event constants. Record the notification parsing entry point as `Stripe\V2\Core\EventNotification`; record deleted objects separately as `Stripe\V2\DeletedObject`. For any case still written as `Stripe\V2\Event`, first confirm whether it is a legacy call, an incorrect name, or a temporary mapping; do not treat it as a current export.

This guidance addresses only the namespace checklist. It does not change the evidence needed for the null branch: explicit null must still be determined from the original input, the prepared structure, and the request representation. The fact that the checklist recognizes a V2 name does not imply that null passed through unchanged; an anomalous null sample likewise cannot imply that a particular V2 name was not exported.

## When encountering old records

Some historical records only say "start checking from Event", while others leave only `event` or an account application event string. For such records, first process them through the old entry point, and add "the complete V2 class name was not provided". There is no need to rewrite them as anomalies in the current checklist.

Other records write explicit null as "empty request". Unless the key and value in the original input are visible, retain the original wording and note that the evidence is insufficient. Do not infer from an empty request that the original was necessarily null, nor use later parameters to reinterpret the old sample.

Only when an old record actually provides the complete V2 name should it be put back into the current checklist branch. At that point, add only the name status; do not invent parameters, a call stack, or loading results that were not recorded at the time.

## Adjacent issues not split out

One type of case has both an old generic event string and a complete V2 class name: the caller handles the old event first, then requests a V2 resource on a subsequent path. The existing records support only storing the two names separately, and are still insufficient to determine whether this coexistence is always caused by the same call chain. Do not write the coexistence itself as a migration failure.

The null path also has one unresolved point: whether different input forms show the same key retention behavior during the same parameter preparation stage. The current approach only requires distinguishing "no key", "key disappeared", "the key is still present but the value changed". It does not provide a conclusion covering all parameter forms.

## Appendix of old examples: generic Event checks

The following fragment is for understanding legacy text, not a V2 checklist sample:

```php
namespace Stripe;

class Event extends ApiResource
{
    const OBJECT_NAME = 'event';
    const ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_AUTHORIZED = 'account.application.authorized';
}
```

It can help confirm whether the legacy text still points to a generic event resource, but it cannot be used to generate any V2 class name or indicate which new directory the object obtained by the caller came from.

There is another outdated shorthand in the old example: "if event is not found then search for `Stripe\V2\Event`." This shorthand is retained as an error example. In the current case, the actual complete name must be saved first; if the name is exactly the old shorthand, do not automatically change it to some new class and continue investigating.

## Content to leave at the end

For the name track, record at least the full class name, where it appears, and whether the list shows the current name, the old name, or no name. For the null track, record at least whether the original input contains the key, and whether the key is still present and still null at the next point where it is observed. When both tracks occur together, they can be kept in the same record, but do not substitute one conclusion for the other.

The old `lib/Event.php` remains the lookup entry point for regular event constants; handle current V2 names according to the list conventions later on this page. Historical steps do not need to be removed, as long as they are not mistaken for current directory rules in new cases.

# Client Configuration and Retry History

This round, we're documenting Client configuration and Retry-After API removal separately. Both fall within the same closeout scope, but the former concerns where the client receives and interprets configuration, while the latter is cleanup of an old public entry point; combining them into one change would let caller differences and the API migration obscure each other.

The tentative plan is to start checking configuration boundaries at `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`. The direct dependency visible in the file is `Stripe\Util\Util`. At this stage, we won't split the configuration array across individual request call sites or change all retry-related code just because we're preparing to remove the Retry-After entry point.

We compared two approaches: have each call site interpret configuration itself; or retain the centralized entry point on the client side and clean up only the confirmed legacy public surface. We'll start with the latter. This is not because we've found all callers, but to avoid expanding the migration scope in the same round.
