versions.body:
# Client Configuration and Retry History

This record will still be looked up, usually not because it provides new configuration rules, but because the two adjacent issues were not combined into one major change at the time: where Client configuration is interpreted, and the scope of Retry-After API removal. The initial draft's conclusion was narrow: when cleaning up old entry points, do not spread the authority to interpret client configuration back to request call sites.

Review retained this decision and tightened the initial draft's wording. `lib/BaseStripeClient.php` is the priority verification entry point for configuration issues; that does not mean every request parameter, every wrapper layer, or all retry behavior is handled here. The initial draft described the "client boundary" as though it were an already closed implementation fact; the existing material supports using it only as the starting point for investigation.

## Tradeoffs Left by the Initial Draft

At the time, the wording most likely to appear was "there is a problem with the retry configuration". This wording conflated two types of phenomena: the caller believes the client configuration did not take effect as expected, or the caller is still looking for a Retry-After API that is slated for removal. The two phenomena can occur at the same time, but that does not make them the same change point.

The first candidate was to have each request call site read and interpret client configuration on its own. Its immediate benefit was that the change appeared close to the request; the cost was that the same set of default values and caller-supplied values would be interpreted in multiple places. A branch added in one place to support the old calling style might also be handled differently from the corresponding logic elsewhere. The initial draft did not accept this direction.

The second candidate was to keep the old Retry-After entry point in the compatibility layer and translate it into settings the client could understand. This could temporarily reduce the discrepancy where "the entry point cannot be found", but it tied two questions that needed to be confirmed separately into one branch: whether the old API was still part of the public support surface, and whether the client configuration was actually being read. The review still does not recommend making these two judgments in the same place.

The scope control adopted was: start by checking configuration from the client object; clean up old entry points only for the confirmed public surface. Here, "first" indicates the investigation order; it does not claim that the client object owns all request semantics. "Only for" likewise limits the scope of this round of changes; it is not a continued compatibility commitment for unknown entry points.

The initial draft contains a sentence worth retaining verbatim:

> Client configuration and Retry-After API removal proceed separately; check the client first for the former, and handle only confirmed old entry points for the latter.

At the time, this sentence was used to prevent a one-time migration, not as a complete API strategy. When it is cited later, "check the client first" must not be read as "all differences are caused by the client", nor may "old entry point" be generalized to every object whose name contains retry.

## Position of `BaseStripeClient` in This Record

`lib/BaseStripeClient.php` was selected as the entry point for a simple reason: the configuration boundary discussed in this round first falls on the client object, not on a temporary parameter of an individual request. The dependency `Stripe\Util\Util` visible in the file header shows that it is not an isolated list of configuration fields. The review did not infer new retry logic from this dependency, nor did it conclude on this basis that configuration conversion necessarily occurs here.

This distinction affected the processing order at the time. If a report says "the configuration did not take effect", first confirm the value passed into the client and the actual call path used; if a report says "the old entry point is gone", first confirm whether the entry point being sought is still part of the public surface. Directly rewriting both reports as "request-layer retry is broken" will only leave the next change without a clear target.

SPH-206 records inconsistent user-observed results for Client configuration. It supports splitting the field description into separate checks, but it did not fill in the entire call chain for this memo. The material for this card was not available during the initial-draft stage, so this page also retains the gap from that time: the difference may come from client construction, or it may come from a subsequent calling method or runtime version.

## Decision After This Review

1. Client configuration continues to use `BaseStripeClient` as the priority verification entry point. Unconfirmed callers should not be changed to interpret configuration themselves because of this page.
2. Retry-After API removal is checked separately against the old public surface. Do not automatically include adjacent code related to configuration in the same deletion batch.
3. When the field description does not distinguish the configuration value, calling method, and version, do not directly determine the modification location based on "the configuration did not take effect".

The second item is the part of this record most likely to be misread. It does not call for restoring old entry points, nor does it provide a complete deletion list for old entry points. It simply refuses to use "being removed" as a reason to expand the scope of changes. If a specific entry point is still referenced, inspect that call and the version it belongs to; if a configuration value is in fact determined by the request layer, confirm it in that request path instead of inferring it from this page.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Configuration issue" as ConfigIssue
    state "Client entry point" as ClientEntry
    state "Keep interpretation centralized" as KeepCentral
    state "Old entry point cleanup" as RetryRemoval
    state "Confirm public surface" as PublicSurface
    state "Handle separately" as SeparateHandling

    [*] --> ConfigIssue
    ConfigIssue --> ClientEntry: Start with BaseStripeClient
    ClientEntry --> KeepCentral
    [*] --> RetryRemoval
    RetryRemoval --> PublicSurface
    PublicSurface --> SeparateHandling
```

The two paths in the diagram are not an implementation call graph. It only preserves the branching used for this decision: configuration issues first land at the client entry point, while old-entry-point issues first confirm the public surface. The two lines can appear in the same user report, but this record does not merge them into a single fix path.

## Revised Working Hypothesis

The initial draft's working hypothesis was that inconsistencies in user environments mainly came from inconsistency in where configuration was interpreted. This hypothesis can still be used to start checking, but it is insufficient to explain all reports. Existing field descriptions do not consistently distinguish the configuration received by the client, the actual calling method, and the runtime version; therefore, the same "setting did not take effect" may point to different locations.

Here, the wording needs to be explicitly revised: nothing in the material supports "all differences in user environments are configuration issues of `BaseStripeClient`". This file is the closest verification entry point, not the endpoint of attribution. This revision does not overturn the choice of a centralized entry point; it only shifts it from strong attribution back to scope control.

Likewise, Retry-After API removal cannot be summarized as "all retry capabilities were removed". This page does not retain enough material to describe every transport scenario, nor does it record all names and calling methods of the old entry points. Early notes placed "looking for the old entry point" and "different results" very close together; when consulting them later, separate the two rather than filling in a unified retry strategy based on that proximity.

## Old Recommendation Still on This Page

The operational recommendation in the initial draft has not been deleted: keep client configuration in the client first; if the old retry prompt is to be deleted, delete only the segment whose public location has already been found. This explains why the cleanup was not expanded into a complete rewrite at the time.

However, "keep it in the client" should now be understood as setting the priority, not as saying that every final request value can only be produced by the client object; "find the public location" also does not mean that any old call that has not been confirmed can be ignored. The former prevents call sites from redefining configuration independently, while the latter prevents API cleanup from incidentally taking unrelated parts with it.

This page therefore remains a record of an old decision: it explains why the scope of change was limited at the time and retains the post-review correction to the original hypothesis. When determining whether a specific call is affected, return to that call and the corresponding version; this memo does not replace that verification step.

# Event Targets and Signature Migration

This page originally grew out of a very narrow field record: the issue name and call name led investigators to `lib/HttpClient/CurlClient.php`, and the investigation then put the regenerated EventDestination, event parsing, and signature compatibility into the same table. That table was not deleted because it genuinely preserved how things were done at the time; however, it conflated "where to start looking" with "where the object belongs."

At the top of the file, direct uses of `Stripe\\Exception`, `Stripe\\Stripe`, and `Stripe\\Util` can be seen. Early records therefore treated the client path as the main observation point. This position is suitable for reviewing content or diagnostics left on the request side, but it cannot by itself explain where EventDestination was generated, nor can it show which layer performed event parsing and signature checks. This misunderstanding is retained here because later review precisely moved away from it.

## What the Old Route Left Behind

The v1 working assumption was that if the regenerated object showed no new differences near CurlClient, it could continue to be observed in the old way. At the time, this assumption was sufficient to arrange one check, but not to serve as the basis for determining that the migration was complete. It expanded "no change was seen on one client path" into "the object migration had no change," so it can now be retained only as historical wording.

The actual sequence at the time was simple: first preserve an old sample, then pass the same event material through first processing and second processing. Record each time whether the result was content or a diagnostic. If the content was the same both times, initially write "no divergence observed"; if one result was content and the other was a diagnostic, do not classify them as the same result just to align the table. Keep signature-related judgments separate, and do not infer compatibility directly from identical outputs.

The old route's recovery record is as follows:

```text
Issue name / call name
        |
        v
lib/HttpClient/CurlClient.php
        |
        +-- Request-side content or diagnostic
        |
        +-- Result left after event processing
        |
        v
The old table once treated two types of observations as the same migration evidence
```

This diagram represents only the historical troubleshooting sequence; it does not mean that the file is the only entry point to the migration implementation. The old sample should still be preserved as-is and must not first be rewritten as a description of the regenerated object; otherwise, during rollback it will be impossible to determine whether a difference came from the sample, the object, or the processing stage.

## Three Groups of Records Kept Separate During Migration

Record the regenerated object separately first. Keep the old sample's name, how it was obtained, and the object behavior that the caller could observe at the time. The focus here is to compare how the old and new objects are accessed, without filling post-event-processing content into the object column in advance. If the object name, constants, or construction behavior changed, record the change itself; if no change was seen only at the current observation point, state the observation point clearly and do not write it as overall compatibility.

Start a separate group for event parsing. For the same input, preserve the content or diagnostic from the first processing, then preserve the content or diagnostic from the second processing. The two records need to show the processing order, but there is no need to fill in stages for which no material is available. If the first processing changed the material available later, the second result cannot be compared with the first as if they were exactly the same input; retain this as not directly comparable rather than labeling it a signature failure.

Review signature compatibility after the event-parsing results. Discuss compatibility only when the material used for the signature, the timing conditions, and the processing stage remain identifiable. If both runs return the same diagnostic, this can show that this set of records revealed no difference, but it cannot replace checking the signature semantics. Conversely, a changed diagnostic cannot automatically be attributed to the client request; first determine whether it belongs to parsing, validation, or a result incidentally left by the old observation entry.

Migration records can be organized in the following order:

| Observation group | Preserve first | What this group cannot replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EventDestination regeneration | Old sample, how the regenerated object is accessed, and object-side differences | Cannot use no request-side change to prove that object migration is complete |
| First event processing | Input and the first content or diagnostic | Cannot represent the result of second processing |
| Second event processing | The second content or diagnostic from the same batch of material | Cannot by itself prove signature compatibility |
| Signature check | The stage where it occurred, comparable material, and the result | Cannot attribute every processing anomaly to the client |

The "cannot replace" column is not a new general rule; it is a correction to the old table. The old table compressed the object, parsing, and signature columns into one "compatible" cell, making it difficult later in the investigation to know which item had actually changed.

## Old Approach and Rollback

The old approach relied on CurlClient as a unified observation point. Its advantage was that it was easy to find and allowed request-side records to stabilize first; its disadvantage was that it placed object migration and event-processing results in the same adjacent position, with no clear split point when a difference appeared. Early records also assumed that simply looking again through the old entry would restore the original judgment. This practice is retained as an old step and is no longer treated as a complete recovery plan.

When restoring the old path, first remove the mixed conclusions added in this round, leaving only the old sample and the original order of each record. Then check `lib/HttpClient/CurlClient.php` to see whether the original request-side content or diagnostic can be read. If it can be read, mark it as an old observation; if it cannot, record the absence and do not fill it in as a transport-layer change.

The sequence to restart after recovery is:

1. Retrieve the old sample; do not rewrite it as a description of the new object.
2. Separately preserve the object-side observation of EventDestination regeneration.
3. Record the first processing result for the same event material.
4. Record the second processing result without replacing the input.
5. Put the signature result into the compatibility check only when the material and stage of the two records are comparable.

If there is already an independent object-side result, there is no need to go through CurlClient again for the sake of formality. Returning to the old entry resolves only one thing: confirming what the old investigation saw at the time. It is not responsible for filling gaps in generated resources, the parsing entry point, or signature validation.

## Retained Old Judgments

> When there is no difference on the request side, regeneration does not need to be checked again.

It was later found that this sentence overstated the observation scope. No difference on the request side can only mean that no difference appeared at that request-side position; the object side still needs to be checked against its own sample.

> If both event-processing runs return the same content, signature compatibility can be recorded as complete.

This sentence also remains on the page as part of the old record. Identical content can only show that the two records have the same form. Without distinguishing parsing content, validation diagnostics, and processing order, they cannot be combined into a signature conclusion.

> If the issue name still points to CurlClient, end the investigation there.

This judgment later caused repeated rechecking. Issue names and call names can provide an entry point, but they cannot determine the ownership of EventDestination, nor can they determine the event-parsing stage. The old wording is not cleaned up retroactively; readers need to know why it once seemed reasonable and where it failed.

The current record therefore requires only grouping and preservation order; it does not assign an implementation location to each generation result. When the material is insufficient, write "no difference observed," "not comparable," or "not confirmed," and do not use a tidier term to cover different stages.

## Short Format for Review

During an actual review, a sample can retain only this section:

```text
Sample: <old sample identifier>
Object side: Difference observed before and after regeneration / no difference observed
First processing: content / diagnostic / stage
Second processing: content / diagnostic / stage
Signature: comparable result / not confirmed
Old entry: whether CurlClient was reviewed; record observations only
```

"No difference observed" must be read together with the sample and location. It does not mean that all migration behavior has been confirmed. "Not comparable" does not equal failure; it may mean that the first processing has already changed the material, or that the stage was not specified at the time. Both gaps should remain in the record.

DOC-20 is related to generated-resource regression and plugin startup and belongs to another adjacent set of materials. Here, retain only the historical relationship among EventDestination, first and second event processing, and the old client observation entry; do not put regression conclusions from the other page into this migration record.

Two points remain unresolved at the end of the page: when no difference is seen on the object side but the diagnostics from first and second processing differ, whether the difference occurred in the parsing stage or a signature-related stage; and under what conditions the observation from the old entry can still be used alongside the new object record. The old document once tried to classify both under the client path; we no longer classify them that way, but this material does not provide enough basis for a new single location.

versions.body:
# Notification Factory and Dispatch Decision

This round, do not combine Notification factory object shape and Typed dispatch veto ordering into one Event class change. Both have previously been grouped under the "notification" problem, but they answer different questions: the former asks whether the instance handed off by the factory is stable; the latter asks whether the veto order after entering typed dispatch is fixed. Collapsing them into one behavior would make a single fix change both the construction and dispatch decision surfaces.

## Trade-offs

Two approaches were considered.

- Use the existing constant `lib/Event.php` as a common baseline, first add the same regression coverage for the factory and dispatch, then converge based on the failures.
- Keep `Event` as a historical reference point, and validate factory object shape and dispatch veto through two independent paths; while either remains unstable, do not use the result from the other to fill in the semantics.

The latter is the decision. The Notification factory cannot yet be reproduced consistently, so this cannot support a claim that a particular event string necessarily maps to a particular notification object. The Typed dispatch issue, however, clearly needs regression coverage in the repository; it should be checked starting from an already-constructed typed notification, rather than relying on the object state the factory happens to return.

This decision also rules out a convenient but unreliable approach: deriving the shared shape of the new notification layer from the object names and event constants of legacy event resources. In `lib/Event.php`, `Event` inherits from `ApiResource` and declares `OBJECT_NAME = 'event'`. That same location also retains `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_AUTHORIZED` and `ACCOUNT_APPLICATION_DEAUTHORIZED` as event-name constants. These declarations show how the legacy resources identify events; they cannot by themselves determine the factory instance's type, fields, or veto-callback ordering.

## Boundaries of the Two Records

On the factory side, record only instance differences that can be reproduced from the pre-call state. If an object produced for an input cannot be reproduced, retain the input conditions; do not write that object's shape down as a rule. When verification is needed, first return to the `lib/Event.php`'s `Stripe` namespace, `Event` declaration, and event constants, then confirm at the actual call site who creates the object.

On the dispatch side, regression coverage records only the stage at which the veto occurs and which subsequent processing does not take place after the veto. It should not determine ordering by comparing object appearance. Conversely, factory tests should not assume that a handler has been called to cover the veto path. This avoids having "object is correct but the order is wrong" masked by a single broad assertion.

## Deferred Items

At present, there are not enough stable samples to determine Notification factory's final object shape, nor has the complete order of the Typed dispatch veto been written down as a public commitment. The next addition should separately provide one reproducible factory input and one existing test path capable of distinguishing processing before and after the veto; only once both can be explained independently should we consider putting them into the same compatibility conclusion.

The interface review for DOC-22 covers version metadata and discriminated-union conversion. It is adjacent to the two decision surfaces here, but does not serve as the basis for this decision.

# Version Metadata and Discriminated Union Plan

This closeout puts API release version metadata and Discriminated union coercion into the same review round, but the two should not share an implementation entry point. The former is a stable read point for information exposed by the client; the latter is the conversion rule applied when request and response values enter the typed boundary. Putting version checks into conversion logic, or making client configuration handle discriminated-union identification, will make subsequent regressions harder to localize.

The initial checkpoint for the client boundary is `lib/BaseStripeClient.php`. The file visibly contains a dependency on `Stripe\Util\Util`, which is useful for checking whether the public client may carry version information indirectly; this does not by itself indicate that the version constant or type conversion belongs in this class. The implementation location should still be determined by the actual call chain.

The proposed direction for version information is to retain an entry point for reading the current release version without constructing a client. Callers should not infer the version from User-Agent, request parameters, or client-instance state, and should not accept an empty value and fill in their own default. This keeps the release version separate from runtime request state; the tradeoff is that a version change requires checking both this entry point and the public documentation that depends on it.

The candidate approach for discriminated unions is to have the schema explicitly specify the discriminator field and its variant mapping, then handle outbound parameters and inbound responses separately. Do not rely on object fields that "look like" a variant to infer the type: the same field combination may have different meanings in different versions. Explicit discrimination adds to the schema maintenance burden, but keeps unsupported discriminator values at the conversion boundary instead of producing a partially correct object after resource hydration.

The plan does not include all scalar conversions at this stage. Existing conversion needs such as those for Int64 can reuse the same schema language, but this round only confirms whether a discriminated union can express the branches it needs, to avoid expanding the version metadata review into a full encoding/decoding overhaul.

There are two conditions for withdrawing or narrowing the scope: if the current version entry point can only depend on the runtime state of an already constructed client, do not commit to an independently accessible public read point yet; if existing callers cannot provide a stable discriminator field, retain only the existing path for discriminated-union conversion and do not infer variants from field shape. Neither case should be masked by adding a new default branch.

Still to verify: which public entry points actually use version information; the versions, entry points, and current results of existing discriminated-union callers; and whether the request and response sides already have independent conversion paths. Decide the constant location, schema shape, and regression samples after these points are confirmed.

# Request Context Troubleshooting Tree

Record the symptoms first; don't change how `context` is passed yet. This old page covers a class of boundary issues called Immutable request context in Runtime Convergence 2026.09. Existing records contain no complete input, exception text, or tool output, so this page can only keep the troubleshooting sequence at locations that can be traced back to code.

## Which Layer to Check First

If the problem occurs only before the request is sent, start from where `request` is created and trace downward, confirming where the context object is created and which call it is passed to. If the request has already been sent but the exception appears during response handling, don't attribute the result directly to the context; first record the paths related to `parse` and the earliest observed change to `value`.

If the same call repeatedly produces different context results without modifying the input, preserve the inputs and outputs from both runs, then check whether later code writes to the object again. If the two results match, continue checking whether the caller is mixing the old and new objects. Here, "immutable" describes only the troubleshooting hypothesis; it is not enough to show that the implementation meets that hypothesis.

## Branches

- **Failure at the entry point**: Start at the location where `new` appears; record the parameters accepted during construction and the name of the immediately following call. Follow only directly adjacent relationships that are visible; stop when you cannot find the next hop; do not fill in a complete chain from neighboring files.
- **Failure after entering the request**: Record `request`, `context`, and `value` separately. First confirm which object the exception corresponds to, then check whether it passed through `parse`. If you can see only the error name, not the call that produced the error, retain the name; don't guess the specific branch.
- **Response looks normal but subsequent state is wrong**: Check whether the context was fetched again after response handling. Distinguish between "the same object was read again" and "a new object was constructed"; record the inputs and lifecycles of each separately.
- **Reproduces only for one caller**: First compare the fields passed by the caller with those at the request entry point; don't turn a caller difference into a conclusion about the client itself. If the difference cannot be confirmed from local code, mark it as unverified.

## Entry-Point Notes

Old troubleshooting records once directed attention to `lib/BaseStripeClient.php` using the issue name and call name. # Evolution of Agent Identity Request Headers

This record did not originally start with a piece of request output, but with a filename that was mentioned repeatedly. The earlier investigation marked `lib/ApiRequestor.php` as the lookup location. The search rationale was simple: terms such as client, agent, headers, and user-agent would all lead people to this area. At the time, someone therefore treated the file as the ownership point for agent identity headers. That statement was not later deleted because it explains why several subsequent investigations all started from the same place.

But path and ownership are not the same thing. A file can be the easiest place to find near a public request entry, or it may only preserve one local adjacency in the request chain. Based on the path alone, it is impossible to distinguish whether the identity information was already supplied by the caller, added by the client's default configuration, or written only during request assembly. The early draft did not explain this distinction clearly enough, so it reads as though the implementation location had already been selected.

The old judgment is retained as written:

> `lib/ApiRequestor.php` is the implementation ownership point for the identity header; look here for the default fields.

This sentence was useful at the time because it let people who had not worked on the issue quickly locate a specific file. Its problem was equally specific. It compressed "search hit," "near the runtime entry," and "field source" into a single conclusion. The subsequent review did not produce a citation or entry snippet sufficient to support that compression, so this page no longer uses it as an implementation description.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

The first discussion actually compared three approaches; it was not choosing among field names or values.

| Approach | Benefit at the time | Reason we stopped at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Directly designate `lib/ApiRequestor.php` as the identity-header ownership point | The earlier investigation already had a stable entry, so follow-up lookup was fast | The file location cannot show that every request generates or rewrites metadata there |
| Capture a response or exception along the public entry, then inspect the adjacent code | It lets us first distinguish what the entry observed before discussing the path | It requires a real execution snippet; without one, a behavioral conclusion cannot be filled in |
| First draw a complete call graph from the caller to the request layer | It might connect the parameters, default handling, and assembly timing | The current materials contain no citable complete chain, so drawing it first would only expand the speculation |

The second approach was chosen. This decision specifies only the verification order: preserve the evidence first, then explain the file relationship. It did not determine the field set for agent identity headers, determine the default values, or require existing callers to change how they pass arguments.

This order also avoided an unnecessary compatibility risk at the time. If we first declared that a field had to be supplied by `lib/ApiRequestor.php`, the caller's explicit value, the request layer's existing default handling, and earlier client configuration would all be forced to adjust according to an ownership assignment that had not yet been confirmed. Conversely, recording the entry response or exception first would not turn unsupported default behavior into an external commitment.

## Boundaries of the Early Draft

In the early draft, "run once along the public entry" was not a completed reproduction. It was only a work plan. The entry might provide a request-header shape that can be inspected, might return ordinary content, or might throw an exception before reaching request assembly. The three cases require different artifacts to be preserved; they cannot all later be written as "the missing field was already observed."

If the entry can observe request headers, record the form of the fields and values that actually appeared, rather than filling in an expected value based on the search results. If the entry throws an exception, preserve the exception text and trigger location. An exception can only show where that run stopped; it cannot automatically show that the identity information was not generated. If neither is observed, state that the observation point provided no usable material; do not use the filename in place of the evidence.

The early draft also came too close to treating "did not see agent" as "did not send agent." The former is only the result of one observation. The observation point may have been before assembly, the caller may not have supplied a value, or default handling may not have added one. The latter is a judgment about the runtime as a whole. They cannot be exchanged, so the reading of the old draft that implied a global absence no longer applies.

Likewise, the appearance of search terms such as `agent` or `user-agent` in the code proves at most that the relevant adjacency is worth inspecting. It cannot prove that the runtime definitely emitted a field with the same name, nor that every caller will use that field. A search hit is a starting point, not a record of request behavior.

## What the Review Actions Left Behind

A caller walkthrough was later performed along the card entry. This shows that the investigation did not stop at path search, but the action itself did not include a citable response, exception, or request-header snippet. The work item subsequently entered processing status, which can only show that someone continued looking through this entry; it cannot show that the source of the identity value was confirmed.

These two records are still worth keeping because they explain why this page grew from a very short file note into a longer decision record. The question was no longer just "where to search," but "which kind of evidence to preserve first, and then whether to expand into the call chain." They are not technical conclusions about the implementation.

After the review, three types of material must always be kept separate: request headers that appeared at runtime at the public entry; local declarations in the code that populate, forward, or read metadata; and whether the caller explicitly supplied a value. They may be located on the same request path, but the existing records have not linked them into a complete citation chain. Using any one of them to stand in for the other two would turn the old path judgment into over-attribution again.

The verification status decided at the time can be written as follows. The branches in the diagram show the order in which material is preserved; they do not mean that any particular output has already appeared.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Path lookup
    Path lookup --> Run entry
    Run entry --> Retain response: Response available
    Run entry --> Retain exception: Exception thrown
    Run entry --> Not observed: No usable material
    Retain response --> Citation check
    Retain exception --> Citation check
    Not observed --> Entry record pending
    Citation check --> Caller parameters
    Citation check --> Default handling
    Citation check --> Request-assembly adjacency
```

The diagram deliberately has no "Confirm ownership" endpoint. What could be determined at the time was which direct reference to check next, not which section was necessarily responsible for all identity headers. If a later review obtains only an ordinary response, it should still not skip the distinction among caller parameters, default handling, and request-assembly adjacency.

## Decision on the File Entry

`lib/ApiRequestor.php` continues to be retained as the local verification entry. This decision accounts for both the search habits in the old records and the practical needs of the subsequent review: starting here will not lose the existing clues, but the path will no longer be written as the sole responsibility boundary.

"Local verification entry" has a very narrow meaning here. It means that the old issue name and call name once pointed to this file, and readers can start here to check local declarations and direct adjacencies. It does not mean that this file owns all identity fields, that all requests generate the same header here, or that information written earlier by the caller must necessarily be visible here.

This limitation is not intended to turn the conclusion into empty wording. It prevents two specific misreadings. The first is that the directory location determines implementation responsibility: because the file is under `lib`, it is interpreted as the common outlet for all agent identity headers. The second is that a single entry observation determines global behavior: because one run did not show a field, the entire PHP Client Runtime is declared not to send that field. The existing materials support neither inference.

For existing callers, the current decision also does not require immediately adopting a new parameter, renaming a field, or removing an old field. Whether the caller explicitly provides identity information still depends on the actual call snippet; whether the client adds a default value still depends on the code adjacent to request assembly. Without these materials, any migration requirement would miswrite a verification record as an interface decision.

## Speculations That Were Amplified

The earlier investigation at one point tended to explain a missing identity header as the request-layer default value not taking effect. This speculation can now only be retained as a working hypothesis; it cannot be used as a fault attribution. It leaves out at least two equally possible explanations: the caller did not provide a value, or the observation point was before the header had finished being assembled.

Another amplified speculation was that, as long as a declaration related to user-agent could be found near ApiRequestor, it would be possible to infer that all requests carried the same agent information. This speculation was not supported by entry material. A local declaration can indicate the direction for reading, but it is insufficient to establish request coverage, field precedence, or consistency among different callers.

These old speculations were not erased from the page because, when a runtime snippet is obtained later, it will still be necessary to know what was ruled out at the time and why it was not immediately accepted. Deleting them directly would make readers think that the current cautious conclusion had always existed, and would conceal why the early draft overinterpreted the path.

## What Should Be Preserved Now

When continuing the lookup along SPH-216, first paste back a complete entry artifact. It can be a response excerpt or an exception excerpt; the important point is that it must come from an actual run of that entry, rather than being inferred from the card title, filename, or search term. If the record is of request headers, preserve the original form of the fields and values; if it is of an exception, preserve the exception text and the location where it occurred.

Then check only three questions through direct references: whether the identity data comes from the client's default configuration, whether it is supplied through caller parameters, and whether it is generated or forwarded at the request-assembly adjacency. These three questions do not all have to be answered in the same record. Confirming one first should not be used to draw a conclusion about the other two.

If the entry material shows that a field is missing, continue to distinguish among "the caller did not provide it," "default handling did not add it," and "the observation point was before assembly." They correspond to different verification locations. Combining them as "header missing" is brief, but it cannot guide the next lookup to the parameters, default handling, or assembly adjacency.

If the entry material shows that the field exists, that still only means it appeared at that observation point in that request. Whether it came from an explicit caller value, was filled by default logic, or will continue to appear in the same class of requests each requires its own reference or repeated-run material. One positive observation cannot automatically restore the original statement about a "sole ownership point."

For an exception path, first confirm whether the exception occurred before, near, or after entering request assembly, and only then discuss its relationship to the identity header. If the exception text does not involve the relevant field, it should not be rewritten as a direct diagnosis of agent identity headers. The early records did not preserve such a snippet, so this page cannot fabricate a failure symptom to support the path judgment.

## Items Not Yet Closed

- The caller walkthrough left no citable entry output, so the complete form of the agent identity headers remains unconfirmed.
- When a field is missing, the three explanations—caller did not provide it, default handling did not add it, and the observation point was too early—have not yet been separated.
- There is no direct citation on which to base whether the same class of calls all passes through the same handling near `lib/ApiRequestor.php`.
- When an explicit caller value and the client's default configuration both exist, the existing materials have no conclusion about which one overrides the other.
- If the field name, default value, or transmission timing needs to change in the future, the scope of compatibility with old callers must still be determined from actual call snippets.

The answers to these questions cannot be replaced by a single search hit. The first requires entry-run material; the second requires a comparison of parameters and default handling; the third requires a direct citation; the fourth requires seeing local snippets from both the caller and the request layer; and only the fifth should be discussed after the earlier items are clarified. At this stage, keeping them separate is more useful than drawing an apparently complete call graph.

## Old Entry Note Retained for the Next Lookup

> Start by checking `lib/ApiRequestor.php` from the issue name and call name. Run the public entry first, then determine who fills the header after seeing a response or exception.

This note is still appropriate beside the initial search entry. It is not an implementation-ownership declaration or a guarantee about field behavior. Someone already started from this path during the earlier investigation, so replacing the path entirely would lose existing clues; continuing to write the path as the sole source would reintroduce the early draft's misleading implication.

This page therefore maintains an old but still citable decision: retain the path as the verification starting point, do not announce ownership in advance; first preserve the entry evidence, then check the caller, default handling, and request-assembly adjacency. If a new response, exception, or direct citation is obtained later, it should supersede the corresponding working hypothesis while preserving the context in which the superseded judgment appeared.

| Resample after rebuilding the environment | Can produce a new path | A new environment cannot prove the original run ever looked this way | Not adopted |
| Cache only the final state | Preserves a brief endpoint | The path before the discrepancy is lost | Not adopted |

- If the second read or run leaves no evidence, the record remains missing.
- When a reviewer other than the author reaches a different stopping point, keep the two observations side by side until someone can explain the difference under the same conditions.

The exit action should not be simplified prematurely either. If it is later confirmed that collection or execution did occur, the exit record can be appended after the current revision; until that is confirmed, the unknown state described by SPHA-013 remains. The cost is that the page will not immediately provide a clean conclusion; what this avoids is a history that looks continuous but actually switched the underlying run.

There is still one practical question: when backfilling state backward from the exit point, which cell should it stop at. The guidance from SPHA-016 is to retain the last confirmable state before failure. That works for filling in the original run's timeline, but not for proving the cache's final state.

# Quality Signal Cache Trade-off Record

The current revision remains the primary subject of this record. The cache has not been dropped, but its purpose has been narrowed: it preserves confirmed leads for later review, but cannot replace the original record or fill in the missing second result to make the sample look continuous.

This decision came from several records that looked similar but could not actually be merged. The earlier short version said only "do not rebuild the environment," without explaining why the cache still needed to be kept or how the exit entry point, regular entry point, and missing results related to one another. After review, retaining the current revision took on a more specific meaning: preserve the original entry point, the stopping position, and the preceding state that could be confirmed at the time; the cache holds only these confirmed fragments and their locations, and does not create a new record of what happened.

## Decided Scope

The choice is not between "the cache or the original record." Both are retained, but they serve different purposes.

The original record captures the entry point actually used during a particular read or execution, where it stopped, and the last state that could be confirmed before failure. It may be incomplete, or it may stop at a single entry point. Its value lies in preserving the sequence at the time.

The cache records information that makes later review easier: the location of the current revision, registered baselines, known stopping positions, and cells explicitly marked as missing or unknown. The cache can help later readers quickly return to the subject, but it cannot backfill results from a new account, a new workspace, or a newly created environment into an old path.

Rebuilding the environment is not considered useless; it is simply not a substitute for the current record. If new collection or a new run actually occurs, it should be appended as a new record of what happened and explicitly state that it is not the original record. Directly overwriting the old record with a green or rejection result from a new environment would erase the point at which the first difference appeared.

## Options Compared at the Time

### Rebuild the Environment and Read Again

This is the easiest way to produce a complete narrative: a new environment, a fresh start, and a new result. The problem is that this is no longer the context in which the current revision was recorded. After the account or workspace changes, even if the entry point has the same name, the two paths cannot simply be treated as the same read.

Rebuilding the environment could also lead later discussions to mistakenly assume that the missing second result had been filled in. In fact, the absence of the second result is itself part of the record. It shows that there was not enough evidence at the time to connect the two stopping points into a causal chain.

For that reason, the approach of "rebuild, then replace the old record with the new result" was not adopted. If rebuilding is needed later, it may produce a new comparison, but it must not overwrite the current revision.

### Keep Only the Final State in the Cache

The benefits of this option are a shorter page and faster lookup. The problem is not the cache itself, but that the "final state" would erase differences between paths. Stopping at the exit entry point and being rejected at the second step of the regular entry point both look like failures; in fact, they occur at different positions along their paths, leading readers to check different preceding states.

Keeping only the final state would also discard the last confirmable state before failure. That cell is not decorative; it is the only anchor for placing the stopping position back into the original sequence. Without it, later additions could easily turn "not collected" into "executed but produced no result."

This option was not adopted either. The cache may contain a brief summary, but that summary must point back to the original entry point and stopping position rather than becoming a complete conclusion on its own.

### Retain the Current Revision and Cache Confirmed Fragments

This is the final choice. The current revision remains unchanged as a reference point for reviewing the original path; the cache preserves the confirmed states and their locations within it; when there is no evidence for the second result, it remains blank. This choice does not allow the page to be made as complete as an incident report just because part of the results is missing, but it does prevent people from later constructing a sequence that never existed.

The costs of this choice are also clear: readers need to retrace the entry point rather than rely only on the cached summary; stopping points observed under different accounts or workspaces must be retained side by side; and unconfirmed exit actions cannot be interpreted in advance. These costs are acceptable because what is being preserved here is the Quality Signal Console's own record of what happened, not an overall judgment covering all callers.

## Records Preserved by the Review

The baseline was registered first in SPHA-004. Later records used a different account or workspace, and the read stopped when it reached the exit entry point. This result shows only that the two read paths differ; it is not enough to show that the difference was caused by the account, workspace, exit entry point, or cache alone.

This changed how the cache should be written. The cache may note that "another account or workspace stopped at the exit entry point," but it cannot present this as a proven cause or conflate it with the original path's baseline as results from the same round. If someone later follows the original entry point and observes a different position, that new position should be listed separately rather than modifying this stopping point.

The review in SPHA-010 came from someone who had not participated in the changes. The regular entry point was rejected at the second step, and the previous assignee had looked only once and did not continue holding on to this check. This arrangement did not establish full attribution, but it did provide a necessary constraint: the original author's results can serve only as a comparison and cannot, on their own, justify using the cache to overwrite the original record.

Rejection at the second step of the regular entry point and stopping at the exit entry point should not be merged into "entry point failure." The former indicates that at least some of the path before the second step was traversable, while the latter records only as far as the exit entry point. If the cache contains only a generalized state, later troubleshooting will lose the information about which cell to start reviewing.

The baseline in SPHA-007 has been registered, but the second result has not been filled in. The gap is preserved here rather than inferring what would happen the second time from the first baseline and the stopping point on another path. The gap means that there is no second result for the current revision available to cite; it does not mean that the run succeeded, failed, or was skipped.

Later records added two more boundaries for handling this. SPHA-013 requires the current revision to remain unknown until collection or execution is confirmed to have actually occurred. This requirement applies to cache entries: without a confirmed action, a location in the cache cannot be promoted to a result. SPHA-016 instead requires filling in one preceding cell from the current entry point, preserving the last confirmable state before failure. This helps restore the original record's sequence and lets the cache identify which part is missing rather than hiding the blank.

## What to Keep in the Cache

The cache should retain three kinds of information: the location of the current revision; path terms such as the original or regular entry point and the exit entry point; and state terms such as "registered," "stopped," "rejected," "second result missing," and "unknown." These are enough to lead readers back to the original record without recording runs that never happened.

The cache should not retain a single, edited conclusion as a replacement for the record of what happened. In particular, "changed account or workspace," "rejected at the second step of the regular entry point," and "stopped at the exit entry point" must not be compressed into the same cause. These are only partial records left under different conditions, and there is currently no evidence that they can be attributed to a single source.

The cache is also not responsible for explaining differences between environments. If a new check aims to compare accounts or workspaces, it needs to preserve its own conditions and path and appear as an additional record of what happened. Having a cached copy does not permit later conditions to be treated as though they had already existed earlier in the current record.

For reading order, the original entry point takes priority over the cached summary. First follow the original entry point to find the current revision, then examine the last confirmed state and stopping point; the cache is used to reduce lookup time, not to bypass this judgment. DOC-28 may be retained as an entry point for on-call staff to a failed run, but it does not change the division of responsibilities between the original record and the cache in this decision.

## Exit Actions and Retractions

Exit actions may be appended only after they have actually occurred. If collection or execution has not been confirmed, the corresponding state of the current revision must remain marked as unknown; do not fill in an exit result just to make the cache look complete.

If a later new path differs from the original path, first preserve its entry point and stopping position. It may be discussed alongside the original record only when the new record explicitly states that it is a comparison under a new environment or new conditions. It cannot retroactively rewrite the current revision.

If a cache entry is found to present a missing result as an established state, retract that entry's conclusion, restore it to "missing" or "unknown," and preserve the original record. If the cache is merely missing one cell for the state before failure, follow the direction in SPHA-016 and work backward from the current entry point to fill in the last confirmable state; if it cannot be filled in, leave it blank.

This decision does not require all entry points to be reduced to the same kind of result. It requires each result to know which path it came from, the cache to know that it has not replaced the original record, and missing information to remain recognized as missing.

# Postmortem of the Unmerged Caller-Side Integration-Test Records

This supplementary entry did not rewrite the earlier entry as a single version. Two revisions were once marked as "current" in the same place; this is the first fact encountered when the incident was entered later. The wording in the old record, the changes seen later, and the unknowns about the scope of adoption remain preserved side by side.

What was initially seen was that the public API regression did not match the old record. At that time, attention was focused on the V2 Core namespace, with the assumption that the migration might change the integration-testing side's interpretation. This line of inquiry later did not receive enough supporting evidence. The client request context can be restored, indicating that the user path returned from its deviated state; it does not show that the namespace change was the cause, nor does it show that the other revision was never adopted.

| Stage | Content left at the time | Handling result |
|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | The same entry displayed two "current" records, and the public API regression differed from the old record | Preserved the entry and the original input; did not continue retrying |
| Comparison period | The network retry budget appeared unchanged | Did not treat the retry layer as the basis for recovery |
| Branch organization | The empty POST body was listed separately as a branch requiring further review | Separated it from the dual-version entry issue |
| After path recovery | The client request context could be restored | Recorded recovery and attribution separately |

The early page described "recovery" as nearly equivalent to "finding the cause." This was inaccurate but remains a useful historical wording. A single path recovery can end the blockage at that time; it cannot answer the ordering of the two revisions, nor can it automatically show that the other record in the entry was not adopted.

## Subsequent Addendum

The materials for SPHB-005 first documented toolchain pinning, followed by an adjustment to the handoff owner. The reason for the adjustment was that, during the testing phase, someone able to modify the fixtures needed to continue handling it. The content left before the return identified only the person on duty, and the output from the exit entry was missing a segment, so the return action cannot be fully reconstructed from this record. This change explains why ownership changed hands midway through processing; it does not indicate who placed the two revisions in the same entry.

SPHB-002 were later categorized as a failure. The addendum notes that the expiration action had already passed and that the exit entry did not enter the queue in that round. This statement describes only that expiration action and the status of that entry; it cannot support the conclusion that none of the callers executed, nor can it establish that either revision had become invalid.

SPHB-007 Review by someone other than the original author began. The reviewer could see that the current result had loaded, but the failure point was after the person on duty. This observation separates two levels: a page or result having loaded is not the same as subsequent processing having completed. The results left by the original author can serve as a reference, but later reviewers must not simply inherit the conclusions.

SPHB-010 When peer review was requested, the maintenance branch was considered complete; it was later discovered that the same materials for the person on duty specified different actions at expiration in two places. No version was arbitrarily selected as correct here, because the retained content was insufficient to resolve the discrepancy. The entry point already referred to two versions, while the handover materials also gave two different accounts of the actions at expiration, both of which made retrospective review harder.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Two current records at the same entry point] --> B[Save the original input and entry point version]
    B --> C[Compare old records with the current result]
    C --> D{Has the user path been restored}
    D -- Yes --> E[List the restoration time separately]
    D -- No --> F[Preserve the divergent state]
    E --> G[Cause still to be confirmed]
```

The "current result" in the diagram is not the same as the "current revision". The former is the result that can be loaded at review time, while the latter is the record marked within the entry point. An earlier draft used these two terms interchangeably, making it easy for readers to think that a successful load could determine which revision was in effect. This update only clarifies the boundaries between the terms, and does not invent collection records that were not preserved at the time.

The impact is limited to the user entry point, comparisons of sample calls, and adaptation feedback in Exception · Caller Integration. The direct consequence of placing the two records side by side at the entry point is that reviewers cannot find a single reference using the "current" label alone; integration discussions therefore need to start by asking which version is involved. No material supports describing this as a widespread failure in the main project, nor does any material support treating observations from adjacent projects as part of the cause.

SPHB-013 call for filling in one preceding state relative to the current entry point, retaining the last verifiable state before the failure. The existence of the task does not mean this state has already been filled in. SPHB-016 record the borrower, start time, and return window for the current revision; this is a limited-scope resource return log, not the findings of an investigation into the origin of the two versions.

DOC-33 can serve as an index for looking up the old entry point's migration, but do not serve as a basis for determining the timing of this incident. How the two revisions entered the same entry point in succession, and which callers actually used either record, still cannot be confirmed from any retained materials.
