# Postmortem on Unmerged Caller Integration Testing Records

Old links still lead people to this entry. At the time, the entry simultaneously displayed "current" records for two revisions; people who opened the page later often saw the recovered result first, then treated that moment as the conclusion of the entire incident. The earliest record also showed this tendency, so it has not been cleaned up into a seamless retrospective account.

The few lines initially written down recorded the deviation in the public API regression, the preservation of the original input, the stopping of further retries, and the later recoverability of the client request context, all in one place. At the time, there was no record of the order in which the two revisions had been added, nor of the scope of their actual use. The short record preserves the perspective at the time, and should not be retroactively interpreted according to today's reading habits as a postmortem with the cause already established.

> Previous account: The difference may be confined to the migration point for the V2 Core namespace; after the user path recovered, the issue was probably contained.
>
> This was the initial working assessment. It put a migration direction that still needed checking together with a recovery. No material later emerged that could confirm that attribution, so it is no longer used to explain the incident; the original wording is retained because subsequent reviews did indeed start with this suspicion.

The "two records" here does not mean that a caller submitted two requests at the same time, but that two pieces of material under the same entry each carried the meaning of "current". The entry label cannot tell us which one was added first, cannot tell us whether they were used alternately, and cannot tell us whether one was simply an old display that had not been cleared away. Unless this distinction is made first, the recovery assessment that follows is easily misread.

## When the Deviation Appeared

When the incident surfaced, the old record did not match the behavior of the public API regression. A complete set of request materials that could be replayed repeatedly was not obtained at the time, so "deviation" was not expanded into a claim that every client had failed, nor was a single normal result described as a complete recovery. What could be confirmed was more limited: people arriving at this entry faced two "current" records and could not use the page itself to choose an appropriate basis for comparison; the integration testing team immediately saved the original input and entry version, then stopped further retries.

Stopping retries was not a technical fix. It merely prevented new attempts from continuing to alter an already muddled situation. What was missing from the entry was the relationship between versions; repeated execution could at most produce more results, not restore the last confirmable state before the failure. The old draft said "stop further retries", but did not clearly explain why. Only a later addendum broke this action down: first preserve the observed difference, then determine whether there was still a need to continue along the same path.

Another thing that was easy to misread at the time was the client request context. Its later recovery showed that one user path no longer stalled at the same point; but it was not evidence of version attribution. The recovered context cannot tell us which of the two revisions should be used, nor can it establish that the earlier deviation was caused entirely by the request context. Describing "recoverable" as "explained" is an error in the early records that needs to be preserved and flagged.

| Object | What could be confirmed at the time | What could not be confirmed at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Entry page | Both revisions simultaneously indicated that they were current | The insertion order, cleanup order, and actual adoption order |
| public API regression | There was a deviation from earlier records | Whether the deviation affected all callers |
| client request context | Could be recovered later | Whether recovery explained the coexistence of both versions |
| V2 Core namespace | Had been suspected of being related to the deviation | Whether it was a cause |
| Continuing retries | Was paused | Whether continuing would have produced the same result |

This table is not intended to make unknowns sound more like conclusions. Anything not captured during the incident remains unknown. The scope of adoption in particular: two revisions both being marked as current does not automatically mean that all callers went through the same path; nor is one later normal sample enough to prove that the earlier record was never actually used.

## First round of response

Saving the original input and the entry-point version was the most effective immediate action at the time. It allowed later reviewers to at least know the state of the page when the deviation occurred. What was saved was not a sample whose cause had already been established, but an entry point where version relationships, user paths, and recovery assessments had not yet been separated. Some wording on the old page was inaccurate, but it preserved the fact that these three categories of information had once been mixed together.

What did not work was prioritizing network retry budget as the explanation. During the comparison, it still appeared normal, so the scope was narrowed; but "still normal" only meant that this observation did not directly explain the dual-version markers at the entry point. It did not prove that the network layer was unrelated, much less justify rewriting it as a cause that had already been ruled out. The old draft stated this more definitively than the material warranted, and its placement is retained here, but its conclusion is not carried forward.

empty POST body was also listed during the comparison phase as a branch requiring further investigation. It appeared alongside the dual-version entry point in the compiled material, making it easy to interpret the two as a single cause. The available content only supports treating it as a follow-up branch, not linking it to V2 Core namespace, the request context, or the network retry budget. No seemingly complete causal chain is added here, only the reasons the two issues were kept separate at the time.

The affected areas were the user entry points, call-sample comparisons, and adaptation feedback in Exception · Caller Integration: reviewers could not identify a unique reference using only the "current" label, so integration discussions had to begin by asking which version was involved. There is no material supporting its classification as a general failure of the entire PHP Client Runtime, and speculation from other projects should not be included on this page.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Two current records for the same entry] --> B[Save the original input and entry version]
    B --> C[Compare the old record and the current result]
    C --> D{Has the user path been restored}
    D -- Yes --> E[List the recovery time separately]
    D -- No --> F[Preserve the deviation from the actual state]
    E --> G[The cause is still pending confirmation]
```

In the diagram, "current result" refers to the result that can be loaded during review; "current revision" refers to the record marked as current at the entry point. Both may contain the word "current," but they refer to different objects. The old draft used inconsistent wording here, sometimes treating the loading state as the entry label and sometimes treating the entry label as the version conclusion. The diagram only retains the processing order and does not depict successful loading as completed attribution.

## What the later cards restored

The later cards did not piece together the complete cause, but they did fill in several key breakpoints. Their purpose was not to add many technical terms to the event, but to give "the entry displays an anomaly" and "which actions afterward remain incomplete" a place of their own.

SPHB-005 first record that the toolchain was locked in, followed by a change in who took over. The reason for the change was specific: during testing, someone who could modify the fixtures needed to continue handling it. The records before the return only identified the person on duty, and a section of the output from the exit entry point was missing; therefore, the return action cannot be fully reconstructed from this material. This change explains why the processing chain changed hands midway through, but does not explain who placed the two revision items at the same entry point.

After SPHB-002 were classified as failures, a supplementary note stated that the expiry action had already passed, and the exit entry point had not entered the queue in that round. This statement must be understood within its original scope: it describes a single expiry action and the queue status of one entry point. It does not say that no exit actions occurred, nor does it say that no revision had been returned. Treating a local gap as a global state is the aspect of the old postmortem most likely to mislead later reviewers.

SPHB-007 require someone other than the original author to verify the result by following the original steps. During verification, the current result can be seen to have loaded, but the failure halted progress after the person on duty. This observation separates two levels: a page or result having loaded is one thing, and whether subsequent processing continues is another. The result left by the original author can be used for comparison, but the reviewer cannot simply adopt the conclusion.

SPHB-010 When requesting peer review, the maintenance branch was considered complete; it was later discovered that the same on-call person's materials specified different expiry actions in two places. The two actions were not forcibly resolved to a single correct version on this page because the retained content was insufficient to eliminate the discrepancy. The entry point already had dual-version semantics, and the handoff materials also contained two different statements about expiry; together, these made retrospective review more difficult.

SPHB-013 require backfilling the slot immediately before the current entry point, preserving the last verifiable state before the failure. The existence of a card does not mean that this slot has been filled. Earlier wording made "card created" sound like "incident state backfilled", and that reading should go no further than the task itself. Without backfilled content, the pre-failure state remains a gap.

SPHB-016 record the borrower, start time, and return window for the current revision. This is a local resource-return log, not the findings of an investigation into the sources of the two revisions. It is included on this page because displaying the current records together at the entry point affects which set of material should be consulted at return time; it provides neither a scope of adoption nor a version ordering.

These backfilled records have not changed the original fact: the current records for the two revisions were once placed together. They merely separate toolchain pinning, fixture handoff, missing sections at the exit entry point, the queue not being entered, review by someone other than the original author, and the return window. The early text treated the incident as an isolated anomaly; later material shows that it involves three types of issues at once: entry-point markers, handoff records, and states that have not been fully backfilled, but this does not automatically establish a single cause.

## Changes in understanding over time

The retained materials are listed below in the order they were handled. Their relative order matters more than the final content shown on the page at any one time, because the difficulty in this incident is precisely that old records and the current entry point were mixed together.

| Stage | Materials retained | Assessment at the time | Later correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deviation appears | The public API regression was inconsistent with old records | Possibly caused by the V2 Core namespace migration | Not confirmed, downgraded to a lead for further investigation |
| Preserving the incident state | The original input and entry-point version were retained, further retries were paused | First avoid overwriting the differences | This preserved the incident state, it did not constitute a fix |
| Path recovery | The client request context could be restored | The user path had been restored | Recovery does not mean the relationship between versions has been clarified |
| Narrowing the comparison | The network retry budget showed no anomaly; the empty POST body was listed separately | Some lines of investigation might be ruled out | This only shows that they did not directly explain the entry point |
| Backfilling handoff records | Fixture editing capability was transferred; sections were missing from the exit entry point's output | Someone could continue handling this | Not enough to reconstruct the original relationship between versions |
| Non-author review | The current result was loaded, the failure stopped after the person on duty | Some behavior on the original path was reproducible | The loaded state cannot substitute for the end-to-end state |
| Peer review | The actions at expiry differed between the two places | One account needed to be selected | Insufficient material, the conflict was retained as is |

The "Later correction" column is not a rejection of the earlier authors' work. The earlier authors were dealing with the incident as it unfolded and could make judgments only from the entry points and results visible at the time; later material tells us which judgments should not be elevated to causes. Preserving these changes in understanding is intended to help later reviewers understand why the old links contain wording that is not entirely consistent.

The earliest version did not provide a complete set of timestamps, and we will not invent timestamps now to fill that gap. The action timestamps in later cards can show that supplemental entries were added after the incident, but they cannot substitute for the exact time of the first deviation. Treating later timestamps as the time of the first anomaly would make two separate pieces of work look like the same round of operations.

"Current revision" on this page always refers to the record marked as current at the entry point, not the latest material the reader is viewing now. This distinction may seem minor, but it determines whether someone reviewing the incident mistakes an archived version for the version in use at the time. The inconsistent usage in the old text has not been removed, because it is itself a risk of misreading left behind by the incident.

## Unconfirmed attributions

V2 Core namespace was initially the most prominent focus of suspicion. The reason was simple: when the deviation appeared, migration-related names also appeared nearby. Proximity is not enough to prove causation. No additional material subsequently showed that namespace changes altered entry-point selection, changed revision markings, or changed the recovery of client request context. Therefore, the old statements identifying it as the cause no longer apply.

The normal behavior of the network retry budget likewise cannot serve as proof to the contrary. It was simply something that showed no anomalies in one comparison. The dual-version issue at the entry point may have occurred before or after the request, or may have had no direct relationship to the request layer; the existing material cannot establish where it occurred. This comparison is retained to explain why the investigation was not expanded further along the retry layer at the time, not to declare that it has been conclusively ruled out.

empty POST body remains in the material surrounding the incident, but no connection to the dual-version records has been confirmed. It was routed to the corresponding handling track at the time, reflecting a need to branch the comparison rather than a determination of the cause. When the same wording appears later, it should be read as a branch observed during the same documentation period, not as this page's final explanation.

The recovery of client request context should be read with the same level of caution. It proves that one user path recovered, not that all client instances used the same record, not that the original entry point had been cleaned up, and certainly not that V2 Core namespace was unrelated. In the old records, "can recover" is often immediately followed by "the issue is over", and the two statements are close in time but differ in their supporting evidence.

## Why recovery was not enough to end the review

In this incident, "recovery" had at least three different meanings: a particular integration-testing path worked again; the current result could be loaded during review; only one record at the entry point remained explicitly marked as current. The material supports only partial observations of the first two, while the third has not been confirmed. Collapsing all three into the single statement "recovered" would lead later readers to believe that the entry-point records had been consolidated.

After the user path recovered, the same input was not repeatedly fed into integration testing. This was not because all issues had been ruled out, but because continuing to run it at the time could not clarify the relationship between the two revisions. The subsequent review also did not overwrite the original state with new green results: the review by someone other than the author found that the current result had loaded and the failure had stopped at a point after the person on duty. This result itself again shows that the statuses need to be read separately.

The earlier account preserved only partial results and cannot explain why the other path worked normally. It can show what someone saw at the time, but cannot reliably serve as a basis for version comparison. Later additions emphasized preserving the minimal input, the corresponding revision, the last verifiable state before the failure, and whether the exit action actually occurred, precisely because the final page alone was not enough to reconstruct the process.

This does not mean that more material needs to be piled up for every integration testing session. For this incident, what was missing was precisely the connection between the entry state, the version relationship, and the exit action. Adding unrelated runtime information cannot turn a two-version record into a single-version record. In contrast, preserving the last verifiable state before the failure gets closer to the issue itself than accumulating more successful results after recovery.

## The old paragraphs are still here

**Outdated:** "As long as the current result loads, the entry can be handled using the latest revision."

This statement conflates the loading state with the entry label. A review by someone other than the author in SPHB-007 showed that, after the current result loaded, the failure remained at the point after the person on duty; loading the result also did not answer what happened to the other revision. The statement is retained as a simplified approach used at the time and is not suitable for determining which version was adopted.

**Unconfirmed:** "The V2 Core namespace changes explain the public API regression."

The initial suspicion was not confirmed. The available material contains no record linking the migration to the entries being placed side by side. If direct evidence emerges later, it should be documented in a separate addendum that clearly states which assessment it changes; this old conjecture cannot be used to infer that a technical decision has already been made.

**Overly broad in scope:** "The exit entry point was not queued, so the current revision had no return actions at all."

SPHB-002 only establish the status of that round's expiration action and that exit entry point. SPHB-016 also require the borrower, start time, and return window to be recorded, showing that return information needs to be retained separately. The old statement generalized a single queue omission to the overall return status and is no longer used.

**Still useful as a reference:** "Do not clear the original entry."

This is not an attribution of cause, but a specific measure taken to preserve the incident state in this case. If one record had simply been deleted at the time, it would later have been impossible to know why the same entry had two meanings for what was current. It does not require duplicate records to be kept permanently; it only explains why this postmortem still contains old paragraphs that appear contradictory.

## Review order

When entering via an old link, first confirm whether you are looking at the historical entry saved in the incident file or the current result loaded later. Both may use the word "current", but they refer to different things. If the page provides only a single final version of the content, do not use it to backfill the state of the other revision at the time of the incident.

Next, check whether it can be matched to the minimal input and the last verifiable state before the failure. SPHB-013 explicitly identify this gap; until supplemental records are found, it should continue to be treated as missing. Do not assume that this cell has been recovered just because the toolchain has been pinned, someone has taken over the fixture, or the maintenance branch has completed its review.

Then review the materials on exit actions. SPHB-005 indicate that the pre-return records go no further than the person on duty, and a segment of the exit entry-point output is missing; SPHB-002 indicate that the expiration action in one round did not enter the queue; SPHB-016 require writing back the borrower, start time, and return window. These three passages should be read side by side. They describe incomplete records at different stages, not a continuous sequence of facts that can be automatically stitched together.

Only then return to the earlier technical suspicions: V2 Core namespace, network retry budget, empty POST body, and client request context. These received attention during the incident, each with a different evidentiary status. Do not combine them into a single failure mechanism just because these terms can all be found by searching the same page.

DOC-33 provide an index for locating the old entry-point migration and are adjacent to this page, but do not confirm the order of the two revisions for this page. When you need to locate materials for a particular part, you can start from SPHB-002, SPHB-005, SPHB-007, SPHB-010, SPHB-013, and SPHB-016; each card fills in only its own segment and should not be treated as a standalone verdict on the entire incident.

## What is still blank

This record still cannot answer the two most important questions: when and in what order each of the two revisions appeared at the entry point; which callers ever used either record. The former determines why the entry point acquired two meanings of "current," while the latter determines how the scope of impact should be described. Neither has been confirmed by the surviving materials, so neither gap was filled with plausible speculation in this write-up.

There is another smaller but practical gap: the exact point beyond the person on duty where the failure stopped was not fully documented. What is known is that the current result has been loaded, and what is unknown is why the subsequent steps stopped and whether this is connected to the missing section of the exit entry point. Combining these two gaps into "handoff failure" would oversimplify things; the existing materials only show that the handoff record is incomplete, not that all subsequent processing failed.

This page is still retained because the old entry point may lead readers to it, not because it provides new authoritative rules. It preserves several distinctions that must be maintained when looking back at the dual-version records: entry-point labels are different from current results, recovery is different from attribution, card tasks are different from completed collection work, and peripheral technical clues are different from confirmed causes. The early materials were uneven on these points; that is precisely why later reviews cannot look only at the final paragraph.

# Dependency Boundary Maintainer Map

This page is still in the old directory, so we start with how it used to be read: people arriving via `treasury-supply-boundary` want to know where the dependency came from, who's adopting it, or whether exiting is an option. The early table assigned all three to the Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit on-duty contact. At the time, the table addressed "don't lose the message," not "who has the authority to make a technical call."

The key fields from the old map are below. They've been kept because old links still land here.

| Old field | Old first contact | Meaning at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency source | Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit on-duty contact | Take the source description and trace back through the existing revisions |
| Adoption scope | Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit on-duty contact | First record who proposed the scope and where the material is located |
| Exit action | Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit on-duty contact | **Old view: the on-duty contact could give an initial answer on whether to exit** |
| Temporary takeover | Person currently on duty | Handle the short-term handoff so the question doesn't go unanswered |
| Long-term owner | Blank | Not confirmed; don't fill this in with whoever replied most recently |

The third row caused the most trouble later. It made people think the audit entry point both knew the source and controlled exit approval. That inference had no execution records to back it up; the old table did not distinguish between "receiving questions on someone else's behalf," "temporarily taking over," and "deciding on an exit." So this version has not replaced the blank with a new name or invented a long-term owner for exit actions.

The page's routing at the time can be read as follows. The arrows show where questions went first, not that the next node had accepted long-term maintenance responsibility.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R[Questions about the source or adoption scope] --> A[Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit on duty]
    X[Exit action] --> A
    H[Temporary takeover] --> A
    A --> L[Long-term owner slot empty]
    A --> K[Handoff record]
```

The old map is still useful for separating inputs. Source tracing should include revision clues; exit actions should be listed separately; temporary takeover entries should describe only the current handoff, not stand in for an owner. When these three topics are mixed together, the on-duty contact can easily keep answering exit questions while tracing the source, and readers may mistake that reply for approval.

SPHC-005 documented one handoff confirmation for source tracing. It shows that questions like these could be picked up, but did not assign exit actions to the same person. The repro item in SPHC-004 was later canceled because the issue had been split off into another experiment card; later records also stated that no execution records could be found, that the page's explanatory text should no longer be displayed, and that it had been downgraded to draft. The old map is therefore kept as a navigation page, rather than supplemented with an explanation that sounds complete.

There used to be an opposing working assumption here: as long as the source could be traced through revisions, the audit entry point could also determine adoption scope and exit responsibility. The counterexample is that source clues can only answer "where did it come from," not establish who accepts the consequences of an exit. This counterexample changed the reading above, but did not produce a new owner list. The slot remains empty.

The usable mapping should now be limited to this:

| Object to address | Entry point this page can provide | What cannot be inferred from this page |
|---|---|---|
| Source of `treasury-supply-boundary` | Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit on-duty entry point | That a given adopter will definitely keep using the dependency |
| Revision tracing | Trace back from project records to the earliest material | That the displayed text alone is sufficient to establish the source |
| Exit action | Raise it separately; leave the long-term owner slot empty | That the on-duty contact has approved the exit |
| Temporary takeover action | The person currently on duty records the handoff | That the person temporarily taking over has become the long-term maintainer |

The verification in SPHC-011 requires navigating from the directory or report to the original record for the current revision and writing the point of failure back into the card. It is suited to questions about "where the link points," not to filling in the owner blank. The direction in SPHC-012 is also clear: look for material that can be used to rebuild the project; if no material is available, hide the explanation rather than add a conclusion. Neither card announced a new assignment of responsibility.

So this map retains two layers of guidance. The old layer still says "ask the on-duty contact first about exiting," because that's how the page was once used; the later addendum limits it to an entry point for forwarding the question. Treasury · Dependency Boundary Audit does not make technical determinations on behalf of the long-term owner. # Compatibility Catalog Failure On-Call Runbook

This page preserves the on-call sequence from a catalog run failure. It originally recorded only three tags, with the handoff and revert actions added later; the older paragraphs are retained as they reflected the situation at the time. After opening the catalog, first confirm that you have the original run, not the summary produced by merging the daily report. Two execution records were once compressed into one line and were later split back out; the handoff should therefore state separately where each record reached.

## Capture the Failure First

Before entering the run, save the original input, run version, and first result. If the catalog page shows a cleaned-up state, do not use it to replace the original state. The old version required no reruns at all; that wording was left in place at the time to prevent the original state from being cleaned up. The practice now is to preserve the original run first, then decide whether to perform a single-condition comparison.

`network retry budget` is still a locator term in the old record. When you see it, record only that the on-call person once started investigating from there; do not use it to attribute the failure to retry settings. Similarly, `immutable StripeContext` is only an item left for verification at the time; this page cannot be used to infer a causal relationship between it and the catalog failure.

Retain the sequence listed in the first record:

1. Find the location where `generated resource hydration` is.
2. If you have already reached `event notification factory`, do not clear the scene or fabricate an object.
3. If `explicit null passthrough` does not appear, stop there and record it as the first failure.

This sequence is not a classification table for all current catalog anomalies; it applies only to the visible path left by this run. The on-call person should not write hypotheses added later back into the first three steps.

## The Only Comparison That Can Proceed

After the original state has been fully preserved, select a recent normal sample. Change one condition at a time, and first write down what you intend to change. The request content, migration record, and caller compatibility path must not be replaced in the same round; otherwise, even if the catalog passes again, you will not know which change altered the result.

If the single-condition comparison reaches `indexed parameter encoding`, record only the input shape before and after that tag. Do not change the catalog entry and caller at the same time just to make the encoding look consistent. If the comparison produces `empty POST body`, retain the empty request itself; do not turn it into another class of sample by filling in fields.

When the comparison reaches `public API regression`, the on-call page has only two responsibilities: mark where the first difference appears and preserve the relationship between the normal sample and the failed sample. The corresponding maintenance path handles the public interface semantics; this page does not turn one failure into a migration conclusion.

Stop local operations immediately in any of these cases:

- Results cannot be viewed further without refreshing permissions;
- Data would have to be recreated for the catalog to proceed;
- The difference has crossed into openapi's public contract, migration records, or caller compatibility;
- The comparison requires changing two or more conditions.

Stopping is not a revert. When stopping, hand off the original input, the one change made, the first difference, and the untouched objects. The original project continues to handle communication with consumers; the API boundary goes to the corresponding maintenance path. The owner slot remains as-is; the temporary assignee handles only the action due in this instance.

## Revert Record

The old rollback section says, "Return to the original entry point, then see whether the catalog opens." This sentence was not deleted because it reflects what was done at the time; however, the catalog opening does not prove that the old relationship has been removed. Now, after reverting this local change, replay the exit action, then check whether the old relationship still appears in the run record. If it still appears, do not keep adding patches; retain the failed sample and stop.

SPHD-004 is a navigation card for the exit action and can be used to review whether the revert has been replayed. SPHD-007 preserve a provenance gap: when there is no evidence from which to reconstruct it, do not add an explanation for this run. The old revision referenced by SPHD-010 indicates that it was removed; the catalog entry can still be retained for the next person on shift to locate it.

## Handoff Fields

Do not write "Restored" in the handoff text. Record the following in order:

- The input and version of the original run;
- The first failure tag, or the fact that the tag has not yet been reached;
- The one controlled change made;
- The disproven hypothesis;
- Whether the revert has been executed, and whether the old relationship still appears;
- Which of `typed dispatch veto`, `agent plugin bootstrap`, and `client request context` is only a pending-verification tag in the old record.

The last three items were grouped together in past additions, but there is no proof that they belong to the same run path. Keep the tags so the next shift can compare against the old state; this is not a requirement to fill them in one by one. If there is no new sample, this page ends at the first failure point.

# PHP Support Matrix Decision Record

This discussion started with maintenance of the supported PHP matrix. Northstar Payments wanted to confirm before the next generated-resources release window whether to keep the existing entry point as the baseline for matrix maintenance or change it alongside the window adjustment.

At the time, there was not enough evidence to show that the entry point itself caused the failures in the support matrix. The existing failure records also did not reliably separate issues into "caused by the entry point" and "caused by reruns." The decision was therefore to keep the existing generated-resources entry point and not make the window adjustment a prerequisite for matrix maintenance.

This does not mean the entry point can never change. If a caller-visible counterexample can be provided later, compare the two approaches again. The counterexample should show a change to the established SDK boundary, rather than merely showing that a particular CI did not pass.

Dissenting view: Some felt that the release window offered an opportunity for a coordinated cleanup, and that postponing the adjustment would leave the old entry point in place. This view was not adopted because the relationship between cleanup costs and the scope of PHP support had not been clarified in this round. Matrix maintenance will proceed based on the existing regressions; the window handoff will be recorded separately.

versions.body:
# PHP Support Matrix Decision Record

This decision preserves the judgment from that round of supported PHP matrix maintenance at Northstar Payments, not a general rule for all subsequent release plans. The initial draft recorded only "leave the entry point unchanged for now"; after review, the scope of that conclusion needed to be narrowed, and the issues unresolved at the time needed to remain on record. It is still often cited to explain why a particular round of matrix maintenance did not change along with the generated-resources window, but this should not be taken to mean that the two workstreams must always move in lockstep.

The original debate was not about whether PHP support mattered, but about whether the maintenance work should also change the existing generated-resources entry point. One side argued for keeping the entry point and assessing each matrix failure individually under the existing path; the other argued for changing the entry point during the release window to prevent subsequent work from continuing to depend on the old structure. Both views treated the "window" as a limited opportunity, but differed on what problem that opportunity should address.

The initial draft decided to retain the current entry point. The rationale was narrow: we had not received enough evidence to show that changing the entry point would improve the support matrix, nor had we received examples of callers unable to continue working because of that entry point. Bundling the two changes would make subsequent failures difficult to attribute: had PHP support coverage changed, had the asset release path changed, or had a rerun masked a transient failure. The initial draft did not require the entry point to remain unchanged forever, but simply rejected making that change part of matrix maintenance without sufficient evidence.

That earlier conclusion should still be retained because it explains where the work stopped at the time: that review was neither a release system overhaul nor an asset directory migration review. Some later read "retain the entry point" as "the existing entry point has been confirmed suitable for all versions", which overextends the conclusion. The original decision established only that, given the information available in that round, the change window was not sufficient grounds for modifying an existing SDK boundary.

## The Two Approaches Compared at the Time

**Approach One: Keep the current generated-resources entry point.**

Matrix maintenance would continue through the existing entry point. Failures would first be treated as signals about support coverage, rather than as evidence that the entry point design had failed. The advantage was fewer changes: if an existing regression could be reproduced reliably, its relationship to supported PHP combinations could be discussed directly; if it passed after a rerun, the credibility of that rerun could also be discussed separately. The cost was equally clear, as the old entry point would remain and those waiting for changes during the window would not get the structural cleanup.

Supporters of this approach did not claim that the old entry point had no problems. Their judgment was that a causal link had not yet been established between the entry point's shortcomings and the goals of this maintenance round. Changing the entry point first would make the matrix records serve two purposes at once: confirming support coverage and explaining a release path change. In a situation that already lacked reliable failure attribution, this would make the records harder to use.

**Approach Two: Change the entry point during the release window.**

This approach treated the asset release window as a synchronization point: since generated-resources would be touched anyway, the entry point would be changed at the same time, and the support matrix maintained on the updated path. Its appeal was that it would avoid postponing a structural change indefinitely and reduce the likelihood that the old entry point would continue to be treated as the default.

The objections focused on timing rather than direction. A window establishes only that there is an opportunity to release, not that changing the entry point addresses the problems in the matrix. Without a caller-level counterexample, the change would first alter an established boundary and only then look for evidence that it had improved support coverage. The review did not accept that sequence. What was rejected was not "change the entry point in the future", but "change it immediately on the grounds of this round of matrix maintenance".

The disagreement between the two approaches should not be reduced to conservative versus proactive, either. Retaining the entry point preserves the costs of the old structure; making changes during the window introduces explanation costs. The review chose the former because the risks that could be confirmed at the time had already appeared in the failure records, while the potential benefits of changing the entry point remained speculative. That choice was specific to the evidence in that round, not an assessment of all subsequent asset release windows.

## Constraints Added After Review

The initial draft understated "the failure records are not stable enough", making it easy to read as meaning that simply running again would restore the conclusion. The requirement added during review was: `CI retries retain the first failing trace and record why a rerun is trustworthy.` Here, first failing trace means the original trace left by the first failure; a rerun must not overwrite it, nor may only the final green result be retained.

This requirement changed not the support matrix itself, but the threshold for accepting explanations of reruns. For a rerun to be considered credible, the record must at least explain why it still represents the same issue, rather than combining different states into a single passing result. Without the first failure record, a subsequent "successful rerun" shows only that the same phenomenon was not observed again later, and does not automatically establish that the original failure was unrelated to the PHP version, the generated-asset entry point, or the release window.

The materials from this round did not establish a new rerun process or list how every type of failure should be assessed. This was not an omission awaiting completion, but an area deliberately left undecided at the time. The review required only that the first failure's trace be retained and that the reason the rerun was credible be recorded. If those two items are missing, matrix maintenance can still continue collecting signals, but rerun results should not be used to support changing the entry point.

## Assessment of the SDK Boundary

The meeting materials used a stronger statement: `Treat observable SDK behavior as the release contract, and require a caller-visible counterexample before changing an established boundary.` That statement was included in this decision to constrain the reasoning that "the window is here, so we can clean things up".

Here, observable SDK behavior means behavior that callers can already observe through the public SDK interface. It does not require every internal implementation to be frozen, nor does it require every generated-asset path to remain unchanged forever. What it requires is this: if a boundary is already in actual use by callers, there should first be a caller-Fang Kevisible counterexample before it is changed. The counterexample must show that the current boundary leads to a specific error, an input that cannot be expressed, an incorrect output, or an outcome that prevents an existing call from completing; maintenance preferences, directory tidiness, or window pressure alone are not enough.

This is also why "the existing generated-resources entry point looks old" was not used as a basis for this round's decision. Old does not mean harmful to callers. Conversely, if there is a caller counterexample, a change cannot be rejected on the grounds that "the matrix has no failures for now", even if the entry point still passes the existing matrix. The support matrix and boundary behavior serve different purposes here: the former helps identify compatibility problems, while the latter determines whether there are grounds for changing an established public relationship.

The initial draft's statement that "the existing entry point can continue to serve as the baseline" should subsequently be understood within this constraint. It is a maintenance baseline, not a permanent endorsement of the entry point's public behavior. We chose not to change it because we had no counterexample at the time; not because we had proved that no future caller could ever be affected.

## Arguments Not Adopted, and How They Remain on Record

Supporters of making changes during the window argued that requiring a clearer counterexample every time would keep postponing structural changes until they could only be handled during a more pressured release phase. This concern was reasonable and was not overturned in the review. It simply answered "when is it worth scheduling cleanup", not "has matrix maintenance already proved that the boundary must change". The same failure record should not stand in for answers to both kinds of question.

Another view held that, as long as the matrix recovered after a rerun, the entry point change could be included in the window because there was no persistent regression. That argument no longer held after review. Without the first failure's trace, a passing rerun result cannot distinguish a transient environment problem, a problem that has not been reproduced reliably, and a problem masked by changed conditions. We did not conclude from this that all reruns were untrustworthy; we only refused to treat unsupported reruns as positive evidence for changing an existing boundary.

Another proposal not adopted was to include the entry point change and all support matrix issues in a single release assessment. This appeared to reduce the number of documents, but would combine different questions into a single conclusion: asset release handoffs have their own cadence and handoff materials, while the support matrix needs to retain failure traces, rerun rationales, and caller counterexamples. The relevant window handoff records are at DOC-44; this decision does not prescribe release actions for them.

## A Usable Formulation of This Round's Decision

In the absence of a caller-Fang Kevisible counterexample, and when the failure records do not allow clear attribution, keep the current generated-resources entry point and continue maintaining the supported PHP matrix through the existing entry point. Do not incorporate an entry point change directly into matrix maintenance merely because a release window exists. For failures that require a rerun, retain the first failure's trace and record why the rerun is credible; reopen the comparison of entry point changes only when these materials are sufficient to show that an established SDK boundary needs to change.

This formulation is a post-review addendum, more explicit than the initial draft and narrower than some later statements citing it. It did not approve a new entry point design, declare the current entry point a long-term standard, or provide a schedule for future windows. It only puts the basis of that decision on record: support matrix maintenance must not use unproven benefits of a window to change established boundaries.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Support matrix maintenance] --> B{Is there a caller-Fang Kevisible counterexample?}
    B -- No --> C[Keep the current generated-resources entry point]
    B -- Yes --> D[Compare entry point changes again]
    C --> E[Retain the first failure's trace]
    E --> F[Record why the rerun is credible]
```

## Matters Still on Record

- Whether the maintenance cost of the existing entry point would provide independent grounds for a change in subsequent windows was not assessed at the time.
- Which caller cases would be sufficient to constitute a caller-visible counterexample was not enumerated in this decision.
- The format for long-term retention of the reasons why CI reruns are credible was also not standardized; this round required only that the first failure's trace not be lost.
- If support matrix failures and an asset release window occur during the same phase, whether a new joint assessment is needed still depends on whether their causal relationship can be clearly documented at that time.

This record can therefore explain why the entry point was not changed along with the window at the time, but cannot replace subsequent compatibility assessments. Keeping these unresolved items on record is intended to prevent later readers from mistaking a limited decision for a completed long-term design.

# Event replay fixture entry-point walkthrough

An early trap in this trace was treating v2-events as a name that could answer the ownership question on its own. It is only the most visible entry point into the event path. Whether a location actually receives the event replay fixture has to be confirmed from the call relationships and how the consumer uses it; filenames, adjacent directories, and same-named tests are no substitute for that check.

This review did not expand the route to cover the entire event tree; it still follows just one narrow, repeatable path:

```text
v2-events public entry point
  └─ lib/Event.php
       └─ one selected direct call edge
            └─ the corresponding consumer in the consumer compatibility matrix
                 └─ the first location that receives the event replay fixture
```

The role of `lib/Event.php` is to anchor the starting point for reading the code. After opening it, first look at the event entry point involved in this question, then select just one direct call edge. "Direct" here is meant to keep indirect references, test helpers, and similarly named event objects out of the trace; it does not assert that the file has only one caller, nor is it intended to catalog all callers.

As you follow this edge, keep two objects in mind: the event object being traced at the entry point, and the downstream consumer that will receive the replay fixture. Names encountered along the way can serve as signposts, but a name containing event, replay, or fixture does not count as a match. The place worth a closer read is the one that carries this call edge through to the consumer.

The consumer compatibility matrix acts as a filter on this route. It can help align the event replay scenario being investigated with the actual consumer, and rule out rows that look close but actually serve a different compatibility scenario. Do not work backward from the matrix to invent call relationships: start with an edge traced from the entry point, then use the matrix to confirm which consumer's scope that edge falls within.

During the review, treat a match in the matrix as a cross-check, not a new entry point. If a row does not match the event object being traced, do not follow it further, even if it mentions a fixture. That way, the trace record can still explain why same-named files were skipped without having to explain each of those files individually.

The first actual consumer is the endpoint this record is meant to find. This means the first place that receives the event replay fixture as a consumer, not the last place that uses the replay results. Later processing, assertions, or presentation layers may continue passing along the same data, but they do not change the ownership entry point established by the initial receiving location.

In the draft, "start from `lib/Event.php`" was easy to read as "this file owns the fixture." That wording needs to be tightened. `lib/Event.php` is the starting point for the trace; it is the call relationships visible from there that lead to the actual consumer. Describing the starting point and the ownership location as the same object would send whoever picks this up later straight to the wrong place.

Same-named files can still stay in the notes, but only as signposts. For example, they can indicate that replay-related material exists in the repository, or help confirm the event terminology being examined; without a call edge, do not add them to the main route. This preserves the search trail without misrepresenting a search hit as a consumer relationship.

If a downstream location needs another owner to explain it, stop this record there. Leave four concrete items: the entry point used to start the trace from v2-events, the `lib/Event.php` reference point, the selected direct call edge, and the corresponding consumer in the matrix. With these, the other owner can answer whether that consumer takes over the fixture without having to scan the event directory from scratch.

This also distinguishes two senses of "ownership" that are often conflated. One is maintenance ownership of a file or directory; the other is who first receives the event replay fixture on the execution path. This trace is about the latter. Maintenance ownership may change later, and the location of `lib/Event.php` does not represent permanent ownership either; this route serves only to locate the actual receiving point.

In practice, keep the sequence short: first go from v2-events into `lib/Event.php` and note the currently selected direct call edge; then use the consumer compatibility matrix to find the consumer that matches that edge; finally, check whether that consumer is the first point to receive the replay fixture. If you have already reached subsequent handoffs or a test-only wrapper, return to the preceding consumption point; do not treat the tail end as the entry point.

Two stopping points need to remain explicit. First, when the matrix only shows compatibility scope, do not fill in fixture handoff details based on names. Second, if explaining the consumer's behavior requires another owner, record the known path and ask at that boundary; do not keep inferring from neighboring files. Stopping here is not a failed trace; it prevents material outside this call relationship from being included in the ownership judgment.

This route also makes it easy to revisit earlier conclusions. If someone later says a particular fixture file is the ownership entry point, simply recheck whether it lies on the direct call edge traced from `lib/Event.php`, and whether it precedes the confirmed consumer receiving point. If neither condition is met, it is still just a signpost.

The conclusion retained so far is as follows: start from v2-events, pin down one direct call edge via `lib/Event.php`, then align the consumer using the consumer compatibility matrix. The first actual consumer reached is the practical entry point for further confirmation of event replay fixture ownership. Downstream details that need additional explanation stay at that consumer's boundary; do not extrapolate to same-named material.

# Client Metadata Compatibility Discrepancy Postmortem

After the compatibility window began, client-visible metadata did not match the original arrangement. The request itself still completed; the discrepancy was first seen in the serialized request capture and only later affected checks that rely on this field for compatibility decisions. This records the state at the time; later client behavior should not be projected back into it.

## Incident Sequence

**Initial discovery.** The capture showed that the metadata for the same type of request did not match the window arrangement. No usable request-failure signal was found, so it was not initially escalated as a transport failure. The impact was that compatibility checks lost a stable basis: they could classify requests that should have been in the same class into different outcomes. The discrepancy did not immediately escalate into a request failure, and the usual failure points therefore provided no direct clue.

**Temporary recovery.** First, handling for that window was restored according to the original arrangement, after which the discrepancy no longer appeared in the capture. This only shows that the visible content returned to the expected state; it does not establish the root cause of the discrepancy. The retained capture provides a before-and-after comparison of the recovery; it records the serialization discrepancy at the time, but does not cover other entry points or show at which layer the field changed.

**Follow-up review.** At the time, a successful rerun was treated as a signal that work could continue. The control point added later is narrower: `CI retries retain the first failing trace and record why a rerun is trustworthy.` Therefore, a rerun must retain the first failing trace and state why this run is trustworthy; it must not replace the original discrepancy record with new successful output. This addition addresses the on-call judgment process, not a conclusion about metadata ownership.

## Judgments Retained in the Record

That discrepancy appeared only during the compatibility window; this is not enough to conclude that all client metadata has the same problem. Nor can ownership be inferred from the lookup location for CurlClient.php; that location was only where the call-name check landed at the time. Observations after recovery did not explain whether the discrepancy was caused by metadata generation, serialization, or the window arrangement itself.

The old note's claim that "recovery meant it was already fixed" is retained here because it explains why the on-call shift did not continue tracing the root cause. When reading this page now, treat recovery as having stopped the visible discrepancy, not as a confirmed fix. If a similar situation recurs, first save the serialized request capture before rerunning, then compare the content before and after the recovery action; without the first trace, the rerun result cannot be treated as an explanation for this discrepancy.

## Open Questions

- It is unconfirmed whether the metadata inconsistency occurred before generation or during serialization.
- It is unconfirmed whether the temporary recovery covered only the compatibility window at the time.
- It is unconfirmed whether the same discrepancy appeared at other request entry points.
